In addition to the basic query logic it contains a fairly involved routine for parsing `/etc/os-release`‑style files and a fallback mechanism that walks a list of script files in the build tree to populate OS‑release variables for unsupported distros. The code also contains Windows‑specific helpers that locate MSYS, MinGW and other environments by probing the `MSYSTEM` variable, using helper utilities to locate installation prefixes. All of this runs in a small, mostly inline‑style namespace, with helper functions such as `GetValueChained` that try a chain of getters until a value is found.

@l./Source/cmCMakeHostSystemInformationC.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCMakeHostSystemInformationC.body: The header declares a single command function that accepts a list of arguments and a status object. It returns a Boolean flag indicating success and populates the supplied status structure with diagnostic details about the executing host system. The function acts as a query interface for querying system information such as OS type, architecture, and environment details, and is intended to be invoked by CMake’s internal command dispatch mechanism.

@l./Source/cmCMakeLanguageCommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCMakeLanguageCommand.cxx.body: This file implements the core interpreter for CMake‑style scripting commands. It validates and executes meta‑operations such as CALL, DEFER, EVAL, and the experimental feature helpers, wiring them into the underlying makefile engine, and orchestrates dependency providers and logging level queries.

@l./Source/cmCMakeLanguageCommand.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCMakeLanguageCommand.h.body: The header declares a single helper function that runs a CMake command. It receives a list of arguments and a status object; the function returns true when the command ran successfully and false otherwise. The declaration is intentionally minimal—only the interface is exposed—so that other modules can invoke the command without needing any implementation details.

@l./Source/cmCMakeMinimumRequired.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCMakeMinimumRequired.cxx.body: The file implements a command that checks the CMake version required by a `<VERSION>` argument. It parses the arguments, extracts the minimum (and optional maximum) bounds, compares the current CMake release against those limits, triggers a fatal error if the version is too low, and sets the policy‑version range while rejecting unknown arguments unless the current build already satisfies the maximum.

@l./Source/cmCMakeMinimumRequired.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCMakeMinimumRequired.h.body:
The file declares a helper that implements the **`cmake_minimum_required`** command.  
It provides a single function, `cmCMakeMinimumRequired`, that takes a vector of argument strings and a reference to a `cmExecutionStatus` object.  
When invoked, the function determines whether the current CMake installation satisfies the minimum version required by the command and reports the outcome via the `status` object while returning a boolean success flag.

@l./Source/cmCMakePath.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCMakePath.cxx.body:
The file implements the `cmCMakePath` class’s core path‑manipulation helpers.  
- **ReplaceWideExtension** replaces a file’s extension (optionally adding a leading dot) and updates the internal path.  
- **GetWideExtension** returns the extension (including the dot) or an empty path if none.  
- **GetNarrowStem** trims a stem to its pre‑extension part.  
- **Absolute** resolves a relative path against a base directory.  
- **IsPrefix** checks whether the path is a prefix of another path.  
- **FormatPath** normalises Windows‑style separators and strips UNC prefixes according to the chosen format.  
- **GetNativePath** produces a native string or wstring representation, with special handling for long Windows paths.

@l./Source/cmCMakePath.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCMakePath.h.body: The header defines a thin wrapper around the library’s internal `filesystem::path` type. It supplies a rich set of constructors, assignment operators, and mutator functions that forward to the underlying path object while performing the usual normalisation and formatting conversions (auto, native, generic). The code also implements template‑based type checks (`is_pathable`, `is_move_pathable`) and a small iterator type for traversing path components. A special case for the SunPro compiler keeps the template overloads from colliding with the standard overloads. The file also supplies hash and comparison operators for use in containers.

@l./Source/cmCMakePathCommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCMakePathCommand.cxx.body: This source file implements a sub‑command dispatch table for a CMake‑style path utility. It parses arguments with a small argument‑parser hierarchy that can bind arbitrary members and parse optional flags (like “NORMALIZE”, “LAST_ONLY”), then performs a series of file‑path manipulations—normalization, relative/absolute resolution, component extraction, comparison, hashing, and variable definition updates in a make‑file environment. The logic is organized into individual handlers that validate arguments, fetch input paths, apply transformations via the `cmCMakePath` class, and finally write results back to the makefile.

@l./Source/cmCMakePathCommand.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCMakePathCommand.h.body: The header declares the public interface for a helper that normalises a list of path fragments into an executable path string. It guards against multiple definitions with `#pragma once`, pulls in the core `cmConfigure.h` header (via IWYU‑style inclusion), and pulls in the standard library string/vector types. The key public entity is the `cmCMakePathCommand` function template that accepts a vector of string arguments and a reference to a `cmExecutionStatus` object. The function returns a boolean indicating whether the path construction succeeded; callers use the status reference to inspect diagnostics or diagnostic codes on failure.

@l./Source/cmCMakePolicyCommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCMakePolicyCommand.cxx.body: The file implements the `cmake_policy` command: it parses arguments, checks whether the command is `SET`, `GET`, `VERSION`, or `GET_WARNING`, and then updates or reports policy states via the `cmPolicies` system. It manages the policy stack with `PUSH`/`POP`, and reports policy status changes back to the makefile by adding definitions or issuing fatal errors when required policies are not set.

@l./Source/cmCMakePolicyCommand.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCMakePolicyCommand.h.body: The header declares a single helper routine that configures CMake’s policy‑handling behaviour. It pulls in the core configuration header, pulls in standard containers, and forwards a minimal execution‑status type. The `cmCMakePolicyCommand` function accepts a vector of string arguments – typically policy identifiers or options – and a reference to a status object that the caller can inspect after the call. Its sole job is to translate those arguments into the internal policy switch state that governs whether older policy rules are enforced or ignored.

@l./Source/cmCMakePresetsErrors.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCMakePresetsErrors.cxx.body: The source defines a set of helper routines that attach specific validation errors to a `cmJSONState` object. Each routine emits a human‑readable message for a particular failure scenario – e.g., missing preset fields, unsupported file versions, cyclic includes, duplicate presets, or a preset that cannot be reached from its file. In addition to the direct error emitters the file supplies several factory functions that return lambda‑based error generators; these are used by other modules to produce contextual error messages without having to duplicate the error logic each time. The code is organized into small, focused functions that keep the error‑generation logic reusable and easy to maintain.

@l./Source/cmCMakePresetsErrors.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCMakePresetsErrors.h.body: The header defines a namespace that bundles helper functions for emitting detailed configuration‑level diagnostics. It declares a handful of overloads that the configuration parser calls when it encounters a malformed preset, an unsupported feature, or a cycle‑inherited issue. Each function takes the relevant name or value and a `cmJSONState*`, and it typically returns an error object (`JsonErrors::ErrorGenerator`) that the rest of the library will log or throw. The file also provides a small set of utility functions that construct specific error objects (e.g. `UNRECOGNIZED_CMAKE_VERSION`) for common cases such as an unsupported CMake version or a missing preset field. All of these helpers keep the error‑reporting logic isolated from the rest of the parsing code.

@l./Source/cmCMakePresetsGraph.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCMakePresetsGraph.cxx.body: The code builds a preset‑graph system that reads a configuration file, expands macros defined in that file, resolves inheritance relationships between presets, and then prints or tests the resulting preset objects. It defines a base preset class and concrete subclasses (Configure, Build, Test, Package, Workflow) that each expose an Apply() method. The system parses each preset definition into a tree of preset nodes, checks for cyclic inheritance, and expands any macro references by replacing them with the macro’s definition. After parsing, the code traverses the preset tree, evaluates conditions that may enable or disable presets, and finally prints a formatted list of the preset objects that survived those evaluations.

@l./Source/cmCMakePresetsGraph.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCMakePresetsGraph.h.body: The header defines a `cmCMakePresetsGraph` type that holds collections of configuration, build, test, package and workflow presets. It contains helper classes to represent individual presets, the files they belong to, and the conditions that gate their use. The graph can load preset definitions from JSON files, resolve preset inheritance hierarchies, and print or query the preset order lists. The public interface includes methods to read the project presets, obtain generator names for a preset, and output the current preset arrangement.

@l./Source/cmCMakePresetsGraphInternal.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCMakePresetsGraphInternal.h.body: The header implements internal helpers for expanding macros, evaluating conditions in a preset graph, and parsing preset definitions from JSON. It declares the macro‑expansion functions and an enum for success, ignore, or error results, a base Condition class with virtual Evaluate, and concrete subclasses (Null, Const, Equals, InList, Matches, AnyAllOf, Not). It also includes helper functions that pull preset objects (presets, workflows, packages, etc.) from JSON values.

@l./Source/cmCMakePresetsGraphReadJSON.c.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCMakePresetsGraphReadJSON.c.body: The file implements the JSON‑parsing logic for CMake preset files: it reads a JSON file, validates the version against the current CMake runtime, parses preset entries (configure, build, test, package, workflow), resolves includes recursively, expands “penv” macros, and registers the parsed presets in internal maps while enforcing version‑specific feature support.

@l./Source/cmCMakePresetsGraphReadJSONBu.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCMakePresetsGraphReadJSONBu.body:
The file implements a JSON‑driven parser for build‑preset objects used by the CMake presets system. It defines a `PackageResolveModeHelper` that validates a string value (“on”, “off”, or “only”) and translates it into the corresponding `PackageResolveMode` enum value.  
A helper lambda `ResolvePackageReferencesHelper` simply forwards this logic for a preset field named `resolvePackageReferences`.  

The bulk of the code builds a `JSONHelperBuilder` for the `BuildPreset` structure. This builder maps JSON keys such as `name`, `inherits`, `hidden`, `vendor`, etc., to the appropriate members of `BuildPreset` using specific helper functions from `cmCMakePresetsGraphInternal`. It supports optional and vector fields, and validates that required fields exist and have the correct type. The helper `BuildPresetsHelper` drives the parsing by invoking the helper builder on a JSON array, yielding a vector of fully‑populated `BuildPreset` instances.

@l./Source/cmCMakePresetsGraphReadJSONCo.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCMakePresetsGraphReadJSONCo.body: This source implements a JSON‑driven configuration parser for the CMake preset system. It supplies a collection of helper functions that map JSON nodes into `ConfigurePreset` fields—handling optional strings, booleans, and nested objects for architecture, toolset, trace, warnings, errors, and debug options. The file culminates in a `ConfigurePresetsHelper` routine that validates and builds a vector of `ConfigurePreset` objects from a JSON value, using the internal helper builder to enforce key‑specific parsing rules and error reporting.

@l./Source/cmCMakePresetsGraphReadJSONPa.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCMakePresetsGraphReadJSONPa.body:
The file implements a JSON‑driven parsing helper for the CMake “preset” objects that represent a package’s configuration in a CMake graph. It declares a series of `cmJSONHelperBuilder` objects that describe the schema for a `PackagePreset`:

* **Output section** – binds optional `debug` and `verbose` flags to the preset’s flags.
* **Variable section** – supports a map of string‑to‑string variables.
* **Preset section** – enforces required keys (`name`), optional inheritance lists, and optional vendor information.  
* **Environment section** – uses a helper that produces a map of environment variable strings.

The core helper `PackagePresetsHelper` accepts a JSON value and writes a vector of `PackagePreset` into an output vector. It returns `true` only if the JSON matches the schema, otherwise it records an error via a `cmJSONState`. The code is a thin wrapper around a templated vector helper that produces the in‑memory representation of a preset graph.

@l./Source/cmCMakePresetsGraphReadJSONTe.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCMakePresetsGraphReadJSONTe.body: The file implements a JSON‑driven factory for test‑preset objects. It declares a collection of helper lambdas that translate JSON fields into the corresponding option structs (e.g. verboseness, truncation, include/exclude filters, and execution modes), then stitches them together with `JSONHelperBuilder` into a single `TestPresetHelper`. A static helper is set up to read a vector of such presets from an incoming `Json::Value`, handling errors via the preset‑error utilities.

@l./Source/cmCMakePresetsGraphReadJSONWo.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCMakePresetsGraphReadJSONWo.body:
The file supplies helper functions and builders that convert JSON objects into the in‑memory `WorkflowPreset` structure used by cmake.  
- `WorkflowStepTypeHelper` maps a JSON string value into the `WorkflowStep::Type` enum (Configure, Build, Test, Package) while generating an error if the string is unknown.  
- The helper objects (`WorkflowStepHelper`, `WorkflowStepsHelper`, `WorkflowPresetHelper`) are constructed with `cmJSONHelperBuilder` and bind JSON members to the corresponding members of `WorkflowPreset` and its nested `WorkflowStep`.  
- Error handling is performed via the `cmCMakePresetsErrors` API, reporting an “invalid preset” when parsing fails.  
- The top‑level function `WorkflowPresetsHelper` uses the vector helper to assemble a list of presets from a JSON array.

@l./Source/cmCPackPropertiesGenerator.cx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCPackPropertiesGenerator.cx.body:
The class wraps an installed file into a CMake‑compatible script generator.  
During construction it stores a reference to the local generator and the file and marks that each configuration should be processed separately.  
When `GenerateScriptForConfig` is called it expands the file’s name for the current configuration, walks the file’s property map, and emits a `set_property(INSTALL …)` line for each key‑value pair, quoting names and values through the output‑converter. This gives the calling build system the exact `set_property` statements needed to apply the file‑specific properties.

@l./Source/cmCPackPropertiesGenerator.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCPackPropertiesGenerator.h.body: The header declares a `cmCPackPropertiesGenerator` type that inherits from `cmScriptGenerator`. It stores a reference to an `cmInstalledFile` and a pointer to a `cmLocalGenerator`, and overrides `GenerateScriptForConfig` to emit the CPackProperties block for a specific configuration into a given output stream.

@l./Source/cmCTest.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCTest.cxx.body: cmCTest.cxx implements a comprehensive test execution framework. It parses command‑line arguments, configures test environments, and orchestrates handlers for build, test, coverage, and upload steps. The core logic is encapsulated in the cmCTest class, which manages test metadata, logs, and output handling. It supports reusable handlers for various stages (build, test, update, configure, submit), and provides utilities for encoding, timing, and formatting. The file’s structure follows a modular design where each handler is a dedicated component accessed via getters, enabling extensibility and clear separation of responsibilities.

@l./Source/cmCTest.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCTest.h.body: The header declares a central test‑driver class that drives a full ctest run: it parses command‑line options, loads custom config files, and drives a sequence of build, test, coverage and submission steps. The class keeps a map of submitted files, lets callers register handlers for each stage, and supplies facilities for logging, timing, and XML output. It also implements helper utilities such as base‑64 encoding, gzipping, and color coding for console output. Finally, it provides a small macro‑based logging interface used throughout the suite.

@l./Source/cmCacheManager.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCacheManager.cxx.body: The implementation manages the “CMakeCache.txt” file: it reads the file, parses key/value entries while distinguishing internal versus external values, stores them in a map of cache entries, and writes back the cache with proper formatting and warnings. It also handles file and directory cleanup, supports persistent properties for certain variables, and offers helper routines to serialize and truncate values when necessary.

@l./Source/cmCacheManager.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCacheManager.h.body: The header declares a cache‑managing façade that loads, saves, and cleans a cache file while maintaining a map of entries. Each entry exposes its value, type, and a map of property strings, with helpers to read/write those properties. The manager keeps a flag for whether a cache is loaded and holds the major/minor version of the file format. It also has small utility functions to format output lines for the cache writer.

@l./Source/cmCommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCommand.cxx.body: The file defines the core command‑execution logic used by the build system. It implements the `cmCommand` class, which stores a pointer to a `cmExecutionStatus` object and uses a `cmMakefile` instance to expand argument vectors before invoking the command’s `InitialPass`. Errors are reported by delegating to `SetError`. A thin wrapper type, `cmLegacyCommandWrapper`, clones the underlying command object and forwards a call to its `operator()` overload so that legacy code can treat the wrapper as an executable command. The implementation keeps ownership in a `std::unique_ptr` and relies on proper cloning semantics to avoid dangling references during execution.

@l./Source/cmCommandArgumentParserHelper.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCommandArgumentParserHelper.body: Implements a helper to expand command‑line arguments for CMake: parsing a string, expanding variables ($ENV, $CACHE, etc.), handling escape sequences, and storing the resulting strings while reporting any parsing errors.

@l./Source/cmCommandLineArgument.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCommandLineArgument.h.body: The header implements a generic command‑line argument helper. It stores the argument’s name, required value count, separator rules, and a callback that receives the parsed value. Its `parse` function examines the argument’s syntax, extracts one or many values, invokes the stored callback, and reports syntax or value errors through the system‑tools error interface. The helper also supplies static lambda generators that set flags or assign parsed strings to user‑supplied variables.

@l./Source/cmCommands.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCommands.cxx.body: The file implements a registration routine that binds each cmake command name to its implementation class. It defines three helper functions—`GetScriptingCommands`, `GetProjectCommands`, and `GetProjectCommandsInScriptMode`—each of which pushes a specific set of command handlers into the global `cmState` object. Commands are split into “flow‑control” and “builtin” families, with a subset marked disallowed or unexpected to enforce policies (e.g. `exec_program` is forbidden in favor of `execute_process`). Conditional sections guarded by `CMAKE_BOOTSTRAP` expose additional commands only when the bootstrapping environment is enabled. The file’s primary job is to populate the interpreter’s command table so that script files can invoke those commands during a build.

@l./Source/cmCommands.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCommands.h.body: The header exposes a single class type (`cmState`) and three helper routines that populate a state object with commands gathered from either scripts or project‑wide definitions. When a client invokes one of the `Get*` functions, the implementation hooks into the command registry supplied by the build system, loading the appropriate command set into the supplied `cmState`. The file is guarded by a single‑include‑guard and contains only the declarations needed to wire the command discovery logic into the rest of the system.

@l./Source/cmCommonTargetGenerator.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCommonTargetGenerator.cxx.body:
`cmCommonTargetGenerator.cxx` implements the core logic for the *CommonTargetGenerator* class used by CMake to assemble the compiler and linker options for a target. It stores references to the target’s generator, the makefile, and both local and global common generators, and caches the config‑specific data structures used for flag construction.

Key responsibilities include:

- **Retrieving language‑specific flags**: `AppendFortranFormatFlags` and `AppendFortranPreprocessFlags` examine source properties (e.g. “Fortran_FORMAT”, “Fortran_PREPROCESS”) and inject the appropriate compiler switches into the flag string, consulting both the source and target defaults.

- **Caching compile‑time flags**: `GetFlags`, `GetDefines`, and `GetIncludes` lazily populate per‑language caches that map language names to the compiled strings of compiler options, preprocessor defines, and include directories. These helpers call the local generator to query target‑specific flags.

- **Collecting linked directories**: `GetLinkedTargetDirectories` walks the link graph of a target, evaluating which dependency targets must be linked directly or via a forwarded path. It honors language restrictions (e.g. Fortran vs. C++), and distinguishes between direct and forwarded targets.

- **Computing intermediate files**: `ComputeTargetCompilePDB` builds the path for the per‑target “compile PDB” file, handling multi‑config directories and special naming rules for static libraries.

- **Interacting with external tools**: `GenerateCodeCheckRules` assembles the command line for a compiler launcher (or code‑check tool) when a language supports it, adding optional arguments such as driver‑mode, tidy, and export‑fix files.

- **Supporting multi‑config & multi‑arch**: Helper functions (`GetAIXExports`, `AppendOSXVerFlag`, `GetLinkerLauncher`) embed the appropriate export flags and version information based on target properties.

The class also implements `HaveRequiredLanguages`, which verifies that every source’s language is enabled in the current CMake state. Overall, this file wires together the infrastructure that turns high‑level target specifications into the concrete compiler options and linker flags used by the build system.

@l./Source/cmCommonTargetGenerator.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCommonTargetGenerator.h.body: The header supplies the core logic for per‑target compiler‑flag construction: it gathers configuration names, queries language‑specific features, and exposes virtual hooks that the local/global generators implement to add language‑dependent include paths, preprocessor switches, and linker wrappers. Utility helpers orchestrate Fortran flag formatting, preprocess flag requirements, and the assembly of “code‑check” rules for a source file. The class tracks language‑specific flags, defines, and includes in its private maps, enabling downstream generators to retrieve the exact strings needed for a target.

@l./Source/cmComputeComponentGraph.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmComputeComponentGraph.cxx.body: The file implements Tarjan’s algorithm to identify strongly‑connected components in a directed graph, stores each vertex’s component id, and then builds a new graph whose vertices are those components, with edges reflecting the original graph’s inter‑component connections.

@l./Source/cmComputeComponentGraph.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmComputeComponentGraph.h.body: The header defines a helper that takes a directed adjacency‑list graph and produces a condensation graph where each node represents a strongly‑connected component. It stores the component mapping, the component graph itself, and the mapping from each original vertex to its component index. Internally it runs Tarjan’s depth‑first search: it tracks visit indices and roots, pushes vertices onto a stack, and pops a component once a root is found. The public API exposes methods to trigger the computation (`Compute()`), retrieve the condensed graph (`GetComponentGraph()` and `GetComponentGraphEdges()`), list the vertices in each component (`GetComponents()`/`GetComponent()`), and query the component for a particular vertex (`GetComponentMap()`). The implementation focuses on efficiency (linear‑time Tarjan traversal) and the resulting component graph is guaranteed acyclic.

@l./Source/cmComputeLinkDepends.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmComputeLinkDepends.cxx.body: The file implements a dependency engine that scans build targets, pulls in libraries and shared objects, constructs a graph of dependencies, and then orders the link entries so that each component is linked only after all its prerequisites are satisfied. It also contains logic for detecting cycles, handling shared‑dependency chains, and emitting diagnostics when an unsupported or mis‑configured dependency is encountered.

@l./Source/cmComputeLinkDepends.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmComputeLinkDepends.h.body: The class implements the algorithm that walks a target’s link specification, records each library, object, flag, or group item, and builds a dependency graph that captures both direct and shared‑library dependencies. It then performs a topological ordering of the entries while tracking component edges, and keeps the original ordering for reporting and debugging. It also flags any items that were mis‑configured for the current build configuration.

@l./Source/cmComputeLinkInformation.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmComputeLinkInformation.cxx.body:
The file implements a single class that collects and emits library‑linking data during a build.  
Key responsibilities include parsing feature expressions, expanding library‑placeholders, normalising link entries (shared vs. static), and building runtime‑search paths.  
Its public API exposes getters for the computed lists: items, directories, framework paths, and runtime search directories, all of which are assembled by a collection of private helpers that walk the target’s configuration and explicitly add implicit directories or framework headers as needed.

@l./Source/cmComputeLinkInformation.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmComputeLinkInformation.h.body: `cmComputeLinkInformation.h` defines a helper class that gathers all pieces of a single‑configuration link line for a CMake target. It parses the target’s link entry list, expands implicit and framework paths, tracks which libraries are linked, and records runtime‑search‑path, rpath flags, and other runtime flags. The class exposes accessors to the computed lists (directories, dependencies, shared libs, etc.) and owns a small internal `FeatureDescriptor` hierarchy for decorating link items.

@l./Source/cmComputeTargetDepends.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmComputeTargetDepends.cxx.body: This file implements a class that analyzes inter‑target dependencies during the generation step. It first gathers all targets from the various generators, builds a raw dependency graph, and then uses Tarjan’s SCC algorithm to identify strongly connected components. The code enforces that any non‑trivial cycle can only involve static libraries; otherwise it reports a fatal error. Once SCCs are known the code rebuilds a final dependency graph that replaces intra‑component edges with a linear ordering (head‑tail linkage) and re‑routes inter‑component edges through component tails to heads, thereby breaking cycles safely while preserving all other dependencies.

@l./Source/cmComputeTargetDepends.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmComputeTargetDepends.h.body:
The header declares the **`cmComputeTargetDepends`** class.  
It gathers all targets, walks the dependency graph, eliminates cycles, and emits a cleaned‑up dependency graph that incorporates side‑effects (language‑specific and custom commands) for a safe, ordered build.

@l./Source/cmConditionEvaluator.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmConditionEvaluator.cxx.body: The file implements a recursive‑descent parser that evaluates CMake‑style condition expressions (used by the `if()` command). It tokenises an argument vector into a mutable list, then repeatedly applies five reduction passes in priority order: parentheses, file‑exist predicates, binary comparators, NOT, and finally logical AND/OR. During each pass it recognises special keywords (e.g. `IS_DIRECTORY`, `EXISTS`, `MATCHES`, etc.) and replaces matched sub‑expressions with Boolean results. The evaluator supports the two evaluation modes (old vs new policy) and reports policy changes through warnings. It also contains helper templates that dispatch comparison operators (`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `==`) via a compile‑time selector. The code is largely template‑heavy and relies on helper classes such as `cmExpandedCommandArgument`, `cmValue` and the `cmSystemTools` utilities for filesystem and environment queries.

@l./Source/cmConditionEvaluator.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmConditionEvaluator.h.body:
cmConditionEvaluator.h defines the class responsible for parsing and evaluating the various forms of CMake‐style conditional expressions.  
The public interface consists of a constructor that records the current makefile context and a single `IsTrue` function that receives a vector of expanded arguments, reports an error string if parsing fails, and returns the boolean result together with a status code.  
Internally the class contains a small collection of helper routines that resolve quoted and unquoted variables, match keywords to known truth‐value keys, and walk through a fixed‑depth parsing tree (levels 0–4) that implements the policy checks for CMP0054, CMP0057, CMP0064, CMP0139 and others.

@l./Source/cmConfigureFileCommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmConfigureFileCommand.cxx.body: The function processes command‑line arguments to copy a source file to a target location while optionally adjusting line endings, quoting style, and file permissions. It validates the argument count, resolves absolute paths, rejects directory inputs, and translates options such as `COPYONLY`, `ESCAPE_QUOTES`, `@ONLY`, and permission modifiers into a file‑mode bitmask. After collating all options, it delegates the actual file creation to `cmMakefile::ConfigureFile`. If any step fails, it reports an error via the supplied `cmExecutionStatus`.

@l./Source/cmConfigureFileCommand.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmConfigureFileCommand.h.body:
`cmConfigureFileCommand.h` exposes a single helper routine used by other modules.  
The header pulls in the shared *cmConfigure.h* interface and standard containers, then declares a thin façade:

```cpp
bool cmConfigureFileCommand(const std::vector<std::string>& args,
                            cmExecutionStatus& status);
```

The function accepts a list of command‑line arguments and an object that will receive execution diagnostics. It returns a Boolean flag indicating whether the configure‑file operation succeeded. The surrounding code base relies on this routine to drive configuration logic from parsed arguments, propagating any failures back through the `cmExecutionStatus` instance.

@l./Source/cmConfigureLog.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmConfigureLog.cxx.body: Handles serializing configuration events into a YAML‑formatted file. It tracks indentation, writes backtraces, checks, and various values while properly escaping non‑printable characters.

@l./Source/cmConfigureLog.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmConfigureLog.h.body:
cmConfigureLog is a helper that writes structured logs for cmake’s build system.  
- It is constructed with a directory and a sorted list of log‑version numbers; the most recent version is always enabled.  
- Public methods let callers bracket events or objects in the log, emit key/value pairs (supporting null, booleans, ints, strings, lists, and maps), and inject arbitrary text blocks.  
- Internally it serialises data via an internal StreamWriter, writes to an ofstream, and records back‑trace / check snippets for a given makefile.

@l./Source/cmConsoleBuf.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmConsoleBuf.cxx.body: The implementation creates a lightweight helper around the standard output streams. On Windows builds it installs UTF‑8 pipe handling for both the normal and error stream; otherwise the class is a trivial defaulted object. This minimal wrapper is used elsewhere to expose a unified interface for switching between normal and UTF‑8 console modes.

@l./Source/cmConsoleBuf.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmConsoleBuf.h.body:
Defines a small wrapper around a Windows‑specific console‑buffer manager.  
The header conditionally pulls in the `cmsys::ConsoleBuf` implementation, stores two `Manager` objects for normal and error output, and exposes a constructor, defaulted destructor, and a `SetUTF8Pipes()` helper that presumably configures the underlying pipes to use UTF‑8 encoding.

@l./Source/cmConstStack.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmConstStack.h.body: The header defines a template class `cmConstStack` that implements an immutable, reference‑counted stack of constant values. The stack stores its nodes in a chain of `std::shared_ptr`‐wrapped `Entry` structs, so creating or copying a stack is cheap. The public API provides a default constructor and operations `Push`, `Pop`, `Top`, and `Empty` that return new stack instances (or the stored value) without mutating the original. Internal protected constructors initialize a stack either from a parent entry and a value or from an existing top pointer.

@l./Source/cmConstStack.tcc.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmConstStack.tcc.body:
The file implements a const‑persistent stack that stores its nodes in immutable `Entry` objects linked via `std::shared_ptr`.  
A `Push` constructs a new entry pointing to the current top and returns a new stack instance that shares the rest of the chain.  
`Pop` removes the top entry (after asserting the stack isn’t empty) and returns a stack whose top points to the former second element.  
`Top` exposes a reference to the value in the top entry, and `Empty` simply checks whether the top pointer is null.

@l./Source/cmContinueCommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmContinueCommand.cxx.body: The file defines a helper function that processes a *CONTINUE* directive during a make‑file run. It first verifies that the current execution context is inside a loop block; if not, it emits a fatal error and flags a global fatal‑error state. Then it records that a continue was invoked in the execution status. Finally, it checks that no arguments were supplied with the command—any supplied arguments trigger another fatal error. The rest of the file simply includes the necessary headers and provides example call sites.

@l./Source/cmContinueCommand.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmContinueCommand.h.body:
The header implements a helper that interprets a **continue** instruction issued by a scripting context. It pulls in the core configuration header, brings in the standard string and vector containers, and declares a single exported function:

```cpp
bool cmContinueCommand(const std::vector<std::string>& args,
                      cmExecutionStatus& status);
```

The routine examines the supplied arguments, updates the supplied `cmExecutionStatus` instance, and returns a boolean indicating whether the continue was applied successfully. The function is referenced in several other modules as the point where an executing script will exit the current loop construct (`foreach`/`while`).

@l./Source/cmCoreTryCompile.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCoreTryCompile.cxx.body: `cmCoreTryCompile.cxx` implements the “try‑compile” feature of cmake: it parses command‑line arguments into a configurable `Arguments` object, sets up language‑specific properties (via the various `kCMAKE_*` constants), writes temporary source files, and invokes the real compiler through a `cmCoreTryCompile::TryCompileCode` routine. The file provides helpers for argument parsing (`ParseArgs`), temporary file handling (`WriteSource`), and cleanup of intermediate files (`CleanupFiles`). Its public interface exposes a handful of utility functions (`TryCompileCode`, `FindOutputFile`, `ParseArgs`, etc.) that drive the try‑compile workflow from parsing to execution.

@l./Source/cmCoreTryCompile.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCoreTryCompile.h.body: The header defines the base class for the *try‑compile* and *try‑run* commands, providing common argument parsing, temporary build logic, cleanup routines, and a result structure that reports the produced binary, log details, and any errors.

@l./Source/cmCreateTestSourceList.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCreateTestSourceList.cxx.body: The routine parses a list of arguments specifying test source files, an optional include file, and a test‑function signature. It assembles a test‑driver source that declares the test functions and builds a mapping of test names to those functions, then registers the driver and the list of test sources with the makefile system.

@l./Source/cmCreateTestSourceList.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCreateTestSourceList.h.body:
The header supplies a single exported helper: `cmCreateTestSourceList`.  
It accepts a collection of string arguments, populates a `cmExecutionStatus` instance with any diagnostics, and returns a `bool` indicating whether the list of test‑source paths was successfully constructed.

@l./Source/cmCryptoHash.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCryptoHash.cxx.body: The implementation wraps the rhash library, lazily initializing it once, and provides a uniform interface for the supported hash algorithms (MD5, SHA‑1/224/256/384/512, SHA‑3 224/256/384/512). It exposes methods to initialize, append data (from memory buffers or strings), finalize to obtain the raw digest bytes, and convert that digest to a hex string. The class also contains a small factory routine that parses algorithm names and returns an appropriate hash object.

@l./Source/cmCryptoHash.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCryptoHash.h.body: The header declares an abstract base class `cmCryptoHash` that offers a common interface for creating, feeding, and finalising cryptographic hash calculations. It defines an enumeration of supported hash algorithms (MD5, SHA‑1‑512, and SHA‑3 variants) and provides factory, utility, and core operations (`New`, `Initialize`, `Append`, `Finalize`) for producing binary or hexadecimal hash outputs.

@l./Source/cmCurl.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCurl.cxx.body: The file implements a small helper library for CMake‑integrated libcurl: it sets up CA‑certificates (from explicit file, environment variables or system‑wide defaults), configures .netrc options (optional/required/ignored levels and optional .netrc file paths), and normalises file:// URLs, including handling of UTF‑8 paths on Windows.

@l./Source/cmCurl.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCurl.h.body: The header declares a small API for configuring a cURL handle used in the build‑system.  It supplies three convenience helpers: one to point the handle to a CA bundle file (`cmCurlSetCAInfo`), another to adjust a network‑relay‑control level and file (`cmCurlSetNETRCOption`), and a third to normalise file‑URL strings (`cmCurlFixFileURL`).  All functions return an empty string on success or an error message on failure, and expect a `::CURL*` instance returned from the included `cm3p/curl/curl.h` wrapper.

@l./Source/cmCustomCommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCustomCommand.cxx.body: The file implements a lightweight data‑object that stores all the metadata needed for a custom command in a CMake build: input/output files, dependencies (implicit and explicit), policy flags, and runtime flags such as terminal usage. It exposes getters and setters for each field, handles inserting a “main” dependency when one is present, and records current policy values from a snapshot. The class also supports appending command lines, dependencies, and implicit depend lists through utility append helpers.

@l./Source/cmCustomCommand.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCustomCommand.h.body: The header defines a `cmCustomCommand` class that stores all data needed for a custom build command: output files, by‑products, dependencies, working directory, comment string, and whether UTF‑8 pipes or a real console are used. It exposes getters/setters for each property, methods to append new command lines or dependencies, and flags for escaping and terminal usage. The class also tracks policy states per policy type and records policy values from a `cmStateSnapshot`. Additional helpers manage implicit dependencies and back‑trace information for the command.

@l./Source/cmCustomCommandGenerator.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCustomCommandGenerator.cxx.body: The implementation parses a custom‑command definition, expands every “$<…>” expression in the command lines with either the command‑ or the output‑configuration data, and produces the final command string. It keeps track of any target references that appear in those expressions so that cross‑compiling emulators can be wired. For each target it generates the corresponding depfile, dealing with the special “gccdepfile”, “makedepfile”, or “MSBuildAdditionalInputs” formats and normalising paths. It also records any emulators that need argument lists and supplies helper methods to fetch the emulator location or an emulator‑argument list for a specific command. The class stores the processed command lines, outputs, by‑products, dependencies, and the utilities that have been referenced during the expansion.

@l./Source/cmCustomCommandGenerator.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCustomCommandGenerator.h.body:
`cmCustomCommandGenerator` encapsulates the logic for turning a `cmCustomCommand` into a concrete set of executable shell commands.  
It stores the command lines, their arguments, and related metadata such as outputs, by‑products, and dependency information.  
The class offers a small public API: construction with an optional dep‑file computation function, methods for retrieving each generated command string, and accessors for the working directory, dep‑file paths, and any optional comment text.  
Internally it handles emulators, cross‑compilation utilities, and tracks which utilities are required, exposing that information through its `Utilities` set.

@l./Source/cmCustomCommandLines.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCustomCommandLines.cxx.body:
The file defines two factory helpers:  
`cmMakeCommandLine` builds a `cmCustomCommandLine` from a list of string views by reserving space and emplacing each view.  
`cmMakeSingleCommandLine` creates a `cmCustomCommandLines` container holding just that one line. These helpers are used elsewhere in the codebase to assemble command‑line data.

@l./Source/cmCustomCommandLines.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCustomCommandLines.h.body: The header defines lightweight containers for command‑line fragments. It exposes two vector‑derived types—one holding a single command line, the other a list of such lines—and two helpers that take an initializer list of string views to build the corresponding objects.

@l./Source/cmCustomCommandTypes.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCustomCommandTypes.h.body: The header defines a small set of enums that drive how a build system distinguishes and processes custom build steps. `cmCustomCommandType` tags whether a command runs before a build, before a link, or after a build; `cmCommandOrigin` records whether the step came from the project files or the code generator; `cmObjectLibraryCommands` tells whether a generated library should be ignored or accepted. The file is purely a type‑definition module used by other parts of the system to decide command handling logic.

@l./Source/cmCxxModuleMapper.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCxxModuleMapper.cxx.body: The code implements the core logic for generating module‑map files that CMake uses to satisfy the compiler’s module‑lookup mechanism. It defines a small value‑object (`CxxBmiLocation`) that indicates whether a module’s B‑module‑interface (BMI) is known, private, or unknown. The `CxxModuleLocations` helper walks the dependency graph to find the path to a BMI and formats it for the compiler‑specific command line. A small helper (`GetTransitiveUsages`) traverses the transitive dependency tree to collect all module usages that must be recorded in the map. The three `CxxModuleMapContent…` functions emit the content for Clang, GCC, and MSVC style map files. A `CxxModuleUsage` helper tracks reference entries, and `CxxModuleUsageSeed` feeds initial references and resolves transitive relationships by examining provided and required modules. The file is the glue that turns scan‑dependency data into the plain‑text format the compiler expects for module lookup.

@l./Source/cmCxxModuleMapper.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCxxModuleMapper.h.body: The header declares a small internal library that translates logical module names into concrete file locations and records the way those modules were found.  It defines data structures for a module’s physical path (`CxxBmiLocation`), the directory context for relative paths (`CxxModuleLocations`), and a record of a single module reference (`CxxModuleReference`).  The `CxxModuleUsage` type aggregates the set of modules required by an object and keeps a map of the module paths that satisfy those requirements.  The helper functions (`CxxModuleMapExtension`, `CxxModuleUsageSeed`, `CxxModuleMapContent`) build the module‑map file in one of three supported formats (clang, gcc, MSVC) and detect unresolved import cycles.  The `AddReference` method is the gatekeeper that flags a conflict when a module is referenced in more than one way.

@l./Source/cmCxxModuleUsageEffects.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCxxModuleUsageEffects.cxx.body:
The file defines a small helper class that keeps a 40‑character zero hash string.  
Its constructor is intended to collect usage data from a cmGeneratorTarget, and ApplyToTarget applies the stored information to a cmTarget. The public GetHash method simply returns the internal hash value.

@l./Source/cmCxxModuleUsageEffects.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmCxxModuleUsageEffects.h.body: The header defines the `cmCxxModuleUsageEffects` class that records a hash string and exposes a constructor that accepts a generator target. It provides two main operations: applying the stored effect to a `cmTarget` via `ApplyToTarget` and retrieving the stored hash string through `GetHash`.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerAdapter.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerAdapter.cxx.body: The file implements the core glue between CMake’s internal execution engine and the DAP (Debug Adapter Protocol) client. It orchestrates a single worker thread that pulls messages from a DAP session queue and dispatches them to a collection of request handlers. These handlers expose a full set of debugging services—breakpoint management, variable inspection, stack‑trace retrieval, and step‑in/step‑out semantics—by interacting with a dedicated thread‑manager and a breakpoint manager that track the CMake script’s call stack. The class also records thread‑level state (e.g., current stack depth, next step target) to decide when a “pause” event should be broadcast to the client, and cleans up the internal state when a debugger disconnects or a thread exits.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerAdapter.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerAdapter.h.body:
The header implements a thin wrapper that talks to a DAP‑based debugger session.  
It owns a `dap::Session` that runs in its own thread; the adapter forwards life‑cycle events (file‑parse start/stop, function entry/exit, messages) to that session, and orchestrates step‑in/out requests through its internal synchronization primitives. The class exposes methods to report program exit codes and to report parsed functions, while internally keeping track of step depth and pause requests. Its responsibilities include:  

* establishing a connection and starting the listener thread,  
* serialising command traffic via the supplied writer/reader,  
* maintaining breakpoint and exception handling via the breakpoint and exception managers, and  
* providing thread‑specific context via the thread manager.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerBreakpointManager.c.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerBreakpointManager.c.body: The file implements a breakpoint‑manager that registers a handler for the DAP “SetBreakpoints” request. It keeps a map of source files to their function ranges, uses that information to map requested line numbers to the nearest function start line, and stores breakpoints per file in a thread‑safe map. When a file is loaded it re‑validates any pending breakpoints, sending breakpoint events for those that become valid. All public methods (GetBreakpoints, GetBreakpointCount, ClearAll) operate under the same mutex for safety.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerBreakpointManager.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerBreakpointManager.h.body: The `cmDebuggerBreakpointManager` class coordinates setting and tracking breakpoints for a debugging session. It holds a `dap::Session` pointer, a mutex protecting concurrent access, and two primary maps: one mapping source file paths to vectors of `cmDebuggerSourceBreakpoint` objects (the actual breakpoints), and another mapping the same keys to vectors of `cmDebuggerFunctionLocation` structs that record line ranges for functions. It assigns incremental IDs to new breakpoints, and exposes helper routines to locate a function’s start line (`FindFunctionStartLine`) or adjust a breakpoint to the nearest valid line (`CalibrateBreakpointLine`). Public operations include initializing with a session, registering a loaded source file with its functions (`SourceFileLoaded`), querying breakpoints for a particular file‑line pair (`GetBreakpoints`), obtaining the current breakpoint count (`GetBreakpointCount`), and resetting all breakpoints (`ClearAll`). The class ensures thread‑safety with the mutex, uses `unordered_map`/`unordered_set` for fast lookup, and scopes all logic in the `cmDebugger` namespace.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerExceptionManager.cx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerExceptionManager.cx.body:
The file implements a runtime manager for debugger‑level exceptions that is wired into the C++DAP session.  
When the manager is constructed it registers two request handlers: one to receive `SetExceptionBreakpointsRequest` messages and another for `ExceptionInfoRequest`. It keeps a map from every supported `MessageType` to an `cmDebuggerExceptionFilter` that holds a filter string and a user‑friendly label. The constructor also seeds a second map (`RaiseExceptions`) that records which exception types are currently enabled for break‑on‑raise behaviour.  
The public interface exposes `HandleSetExceptionBreakpointsRequest`, which clears the current enabled set and records the new filters supplied by a request; `HandleExceptionInfoRequest` returns the description of whatever exception is currently pending (if any); `HandleInitializeRequest` populates the debugger‑protocol with the list of available filters; `RaiseExceptionIfAny` is called by other parts of the debugger when an exception occurs, and returns a `StoppedEvent` to pause execution if the filter is active; and `ClearAll` wipes the current enabled set.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerExceptionManager.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerExceptionManager.h.body: The header declares a `cmDebuggerExceptionManager` class that stores exception‑filter mappings and a mutex‑protected map of known exception identifiers. It keeps a pointer to a DAP session, manages a `cm::optional<cmDebuggerException>` that holds the most recent exception, and offers the public operations needed during a debugging session: initializing the exception list, raising an exception when a breakpoint is hit, clearing the state, and querying the current exception. The implementation relies on a custom `MessageTypeHash` functor so that older C++ standard libraries can hash the `MessageType` enum for the `unordered_map`.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerPosixPipeConnection.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerPosixPipeConnection.body:
Implemented as a Unix‑domain socket wrapper that accepts a single client connection and then exchanges byte streams over the resulting file‑descriptor.  
The server side builds a socket, binds it to the supplied path, and listens for a single connection. When a client connects the descriptor is stored and the listening socket is closed.  
The client side simply creates a socket and connects to that path.  
Both sides expose `read()` and `write()` that forward to the underlying file descriptor and close the descriptor on error or zero‑length read. The destructor guarantees the descriptor is closed.  
The code also keeps a simple boolean flag (`StartedListening`) to signal that the listening socket is active. The implementation uses only standard POSIX APIs (socket, bind, listen, accept, read, write, close, and unlink) and handles errors by returning `false` or throwing exceptions with descriptive `strerror(errno)` messages.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerPosixPipeConnection.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerPosixPipeConnection.body:
The header defines two POSIX‑specific pipe‑based connection classes that implement dap::ReaderWriter.  
`cmDebuggerPipeConnection_POSIX` acts as the server side: it creates a named pipe, listens on a socket, accepts a client, and exposes a shared reader/writer pair for the debugger adapter to use.  
`cmDebuggerPipeClient_POSIX` represents the client side: it connects to an existing pipe, then forwards read/write calls directly through the local file descriptor. Both classes maintain the file descriptor, state flags, and expose helper methods for closing the listening socket and synchronising test start‑up via a promise.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerProtocol.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerProtocol.cxx.body: The file supplies a set of “type‑info” registrations for the protocol structs used by the CMake debugger. It declares the fields that describe the capabilities and configuration options exposed by the protocol, such as breakpoint types, memory‑read/write, stack‑trace requests, and client‑side configuration data. All fields are registered via the `DAP_IMPLEMENT_STRUCT_TYPEINFO` macro inside the `dap` namespace, so the generated metadata is available to the protocol engine for serialization and introspection.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerProtocol.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerProtocol.h.body: The header declares the structures for the CMake debugging protocol. It defines a `CMakeVersion` struct, an `CMakeInitializeResponse` that lists optional capabilities of a debug adapter via a set of boolean flags, and a `CMakeInitializeRequest` that carries client‑side configuration. All of these structures inherit from generic `Request`/`Response` types, and the file relies on the `DAP_DECLARE_STRUCT_TYPEINFO` macro to expose type information. The code lives in the `dap` namespace and is used to exchange initialization data between a client and a CMake debug adapter.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerSourceBreakpoint.cx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerSourceBreakpoint.cx.body: This module defines a constructor that assigns a unique identifier and source line number to internal members for use by the debugging framework.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerSourceBreakpoint.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerSourceBreakpoint.h.body: The header defines a lightweight `cmDebuggerSourceBreakpoint` class in the `cmDebugger` namespace. It stores an identifier, a source‑line number, and a validity flag, exposing a constructor, simple accessors, a setter for the line number, and a method to invalidate the breakpoint.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerStackFrame.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerStackFrame.cxx.body: The file implements the `cmDebuggerStackFrame` class: it creates a uniquely‑identified frame (incrementing a static atomic counter in the constructor), stores the path of the source file and the supplied `cmListFileFunction` wrapper, and exposes a `GetLine()` helper that simply forwards to the wrapped function’s line number. The class is scoped in the `cmDebugger` namespace and relies on `<utility>` and `cmListFileCache.h` for its data handling.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerStackFrame.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerStackFrame.h.body:
The header declares a tiny value‑type helper that represents a single frame in a debugger’s stack trace.  
It keeps a globally incrementing `NextId` to give each instance a unique 64‑bit identifier.  
A frame records the source file name, the line number (via `GetLine()`), and a reference to the function object that produced the call.  
The constructor wires the supplied `cmMakefile` and `cmListFileFunction` into the member pointers, while the accessor methods simply return the stored data. The class is deliberately light‑weight so that callers can embed it in larger stack‑tracing logic without imposing heavy construction or copy semantics.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerThread.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerThread.cxx.body: The file implements a thread‑level debugger context that keeps a stack of `cmDebuggerStackFrame` objects, exposes helper APIs for the Debug Adapter Protocol (DAP) and exposes thread‑specific scopes/variables. It owns a `cmDebuggerVariablesManager` instance to create and cache variable collections per frame, and lazily creates a “locals” scope when a frame is first requested. All stack‑frame modifications and read operations lock a mutex to keep the structure thread‑safe. When a scopes request comes in, the code either returns an existing cache or constructs a fresh local‑variables instance, registering it in `FrameVariables`. Stack‑trace responses are assembled by iterating over the stored frames in reverse order. The implementation relies on `dap::ScopesResponse`, `dap::VariablesResponse` and `dap::StackTraceResponse` structures to communicate with the DAP server.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerThread.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerThread.h.body:
The header defines a `cmDebugger::cmDebuggerThread` type that encapsulates a debugger thread’s identity and its execution context.  
It keeps a list of `cmDebuggerStackFrame` objects, a map from frame IDs to those frames, and a mutex to guard concurrent access.  
It records the scopes that belong to each frame and the variables that belong to each frame, delegating variable handling to a `cmDebuggerVariablesManager`.  
Public members provide helpers to push/pop stack frames, query the top or a specific frame, and expose the current stack depth.  
Additionally, the friend helper creates a `dap::StackTraceResponse` from a thread snapshot, and the class offers helpers that return a `dap::ScopesResponse` and a `dap::VariablesResponse` for a given frame.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerThreadManager.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerThreadManager.cxx.body: The file implements a lightweight manager that tracks active debugger threads. It uses an atomic counter to assign monotonically increasing identifiers when a new thread is created, then stores the shared pointer in a container. Threads are removed by matching the shared pointer. When queried for a stack‑trace response it performs a single pass lookup and forwards the request to the thread instance, returning an optional value that may be empty if the ID is unknown. The implementation relies on standard containers and shared pointers to keep the manager thread‑safe and efficient.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerThreadManager.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerThreadManager.h.body: The header declares a `cmDebuggerThreadManager` that maintains a list of `cmDebuggerThread` instances, assigns each thread a unique ID using a static atomic counter, and exposes operations to create a new thread, remove an existing one, and query the stack‑trace information associated with a particular thread ID.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerVariables.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerVariables.cxx.body:
The file implements a lightweight variable‑provider class that registers itself with a variable‑manager.  
When a request arrives, it calls a private handler that returns a list of `dap::Variable` objects built either from a supplied key/value extractor or from any child variable sets that were added.  
The class keeps a thread‑safe atomic counter to give each instance a unique ID, and optionally sorts the resulting list before returning it.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerVariables.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerVariables.h.body: The header declares a `cmDebuggerVariables` object that holds a unique id, name, and value string. It optionally accepts a callback that supplies key‑value pairs and keeps a shared pointer to a `VariablesManager`. The class can add, clear, and enumerate sub‑variables while optionally sorting them, and exposes helpers for constructing `cmDebuggerVariableEntry` instances from primitives.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerVariablesHelper.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerVariablesHelper.cxx.body: The file implements a collection of factory helpers that generate `cmDebuggerVariables` objects populated with contextual data from various CMake entities—targets, tests, file sets, and the current stack frame. Each helper builds a map of variable names to values (often stringified lists or values) and wires them together as sub‑variables for nested structures, enabling the debugger UI to enumerate and edit the rich metadata exposed during a debugging session.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerVariablesHelper.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerVariablesHelper.h.body: Provides a collection of factory methods that build a `cmDebuggerVariables` object from a variety of sources (name‑value lists, file sets, tests, targets, etc.) and exposes them as static `Create*IfAny` overloads. The helper returns a `std::shared_ptr<cmDebuggerVariables>` and internally wires up the supplied arguments into the appropriate variable set.

@l./Source/cmDebuggerVariablesManager.cx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerVariablesManager.cx.body: Handles registration of request‑handlers keyed by an ID, stores them in a map, and dispatches incoming variable‑requests to the stored handler when a matching ID is found, returning the handler’s array of variables (or an empty array if none is registered).

@l./Source/cmDebuggerVariablesManager.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDebuggerVariablesManager.h.body:
This header defines a tiny manager that keeps a map from request IDs to callbacks that, when invoked, return an array of `dap::Variable`s.  
The public interface lets callers register or remove a handler and then ask the manager to serve a `VariablesRequest`, which forwards the request to the stored callback and returns the result.  
The class is deliberately light‑weight; it just stores the handlers and forwards calls, no heavy logic.

@l./Source/cmDefinePropertyCommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDefinePropertyCommand.cxx.body: The file implements a helper that, given a vector of arguments, parses the first token to determine the property scope (GLOBAL, DIRECTORY, TARGET, etc.), extracts the property name and documentation strings via an `ArgumentParser`, validates that required fields are present and that the arguments conform to the expected rules (e.g. `INITIALIZE_FROM_VARIABLE` only allowed for TARGET scope and that the variable name ends with the property name), and finally registers the property in the global `cmMakefile` state through `DefineProperty`.

@l./Source/cmDefinePropertyCommand.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDefinePropertyCommand.h.body: The header declares a helper that takes a vector of string arguments and reports success through a status object; it is the entry point for the property‑definition command used by the rest of the CMake system.

@l./Source/cmDefinitions.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDefinitions.cxx.body: cmDefinitions.cxx implements a hierarchical lookup system for string definitions. It stores definitions in a map keyed by string_view and supports searching a stack of such maps. The core routine `GetInternal` walks the stack recursively; when a key is found it returns the associated value, otherwise it recurses until the end of the stack. If the `raise` flag is true and no definition is found, the function will insert a new entry into the current map, effectively “raising” the definition at that level. `Get` and `Raise` expose the public interface: `Get` returns a pointer to the definition’s value or null, while `Raise` forces an insertion when a definition is missing. The helper functions `MakeClosure` and `ClosureKeys` build a new definition set from the stack, filtering out entries that are explicitly unset. `Set` and `Unset` simply modify the current map. This design keeps lookups efficient via unordered_map lookups, but the recursive stack traversal may stack overflow in pathological cases; adding tail‑recursion or loop‑based search would mitigate deep recursion. The use of `string_view` avoids unnecessary copies, yet care must be taken to ensure the underlying strings outlive the views. Security-wise, the code does not perform any obvious injection risk, but untrusted strings into the map can grow memory if abused. Performance wise the recursive search can be linear in depth; caching results via the local `raise` insertion can amortize repeated lookups. Overall the module is compact and functional, but adding explicit error handling and reducing recursion depth would improve robustness.

@l./Source/cmDefinitions.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDefinitions.h.body:
cmDefinitions.h implements a lightweight variable‑definition manager for a CMake‑style scope tree.  
The `cmDefinitions` class holds a map from string keys to values (`Def` objects) and exposes static helpers (`Get`, `Raise`, `HasKey`, `ClosureKeys`, `MakeClosure`) to walk a linked‑tree of scopes.  
Instance methods `Set` and `Unset` mutate the current scope’s map, while `GetInternal` provides the internal lookup logic used by the static functions.

@l./Source/cmDependencyProvider.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDependencyProvider.h.body: The file defines a lightweight helper that stores a command string and a list of supported “dependency‑handling” methods. It exposes accessors for the command, for the list of methods, and a small helper that answers whether a particular method is available. The implementation is a thin wrapper around a std::string and std::vector, with no complex logic.

@l./Source/cmDepends.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDepends.cxx.body:
The file implements a helper that writes, validates, and cleans dependency files used by the CMake build system.  
When a build is requested it gathers the source‑to‑object pairs declared in the makefile, writes the mapping of each object file to the sources that depend on it, and writes two distinct dependency files (one for the public dependency map and one for internal caching).  
During a rebuild it checks whether any of those source files has changed; if a source is newer than its dependent object or missing, the helper removes the affected dependency file so that the affected object will be regenerated.  The class is designed to be overridden for language‑specific handling of include paths and dependency writing.

@l./Source/cmDepends.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDepends.h.body: This header defines a base class that handles scanning source files to build a dependency map and serialises it to a “.depends.make” file. Subclasses plug in language‑specific logic, while the base keeps track of file‑time caches, language tags, and target directories, and offers facilities to clear, re‑write, or validate existing dependency listings.

@l./Source/cmDependsC.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDependsC.cxx.body:
`cmDependsC.cxx` implements a dependency‑resolution helper for the CMake build system.  
Its constructor loads a cached list of header files and their include locations, then builds regexes tailored to the target language (C, C++, etc.) to locate `#include` or `#import` lines.  
During scanning, it follows include paths, resolves quoted‑include files, and collects a dependency graph. The gathered dependency set is serialized back to the cache file on destruction. The helper also supports user‑defined transform rules that rewrite include directives on the fly.  
The class drives the generation of “makefile” dependency lines for the local Unix‑style generator, writing both the normal and internal “intermediate” dependency files.

@l./Source/cmDependsC.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDependsC.h.body:
cmDependsC implements a dependency‑scanner for C/C++ sources.  
It parses `#include` directives with a set of pre‑compiled regular‑expressions and rewrites matched lines according to a transform table.  
The class keeps a cache of headers that have already been processed, records which files were actually seen, and emits a dependency list to the makefile and an auxiliary cache file for future scans.

@l./Source/cmDependsCompiler.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDependsCompiler.cxx.body: The file implements a helper that stitches the results of a compiler‑generated dependency file into the build system’s in‑memory dependency graph. It reads an intermediate “internal” list of already‑known dependencies, merges that with fresh data from a set of compiler‑produced files (supporting gcc‑style depfiles, custom formats, and MSVC depfiles), and then emits two make‑compatible files: one with the actual dependency arrows and one that records each target’s prerequisites for later reuse. It also offers a cleanup routine that deletes the temporary dependency files once they’re no longer needed.

@l./Source/cmDependsCompiler.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDependsCompiler.h.body:
cmDependsCompiler.h defines a helper that keeps the compiler‑generated dependency file (compiler_depends.make) in sync with a target object.  
Its public interface lets callers set verbosity, attach a local‑path converter (via a `cmLocalUnixMakefileGenerator3`), then query whether a target’s dependency list is already current (`CheckDependencies`) or needs rewriting (`WriteDependencies`). A cleanup method (`ClearDependencies`) marks a target’s deps as stale so the next build will regenerate them. The class internally holds a verbosity flag and a pointer to the local generator used for relative‑path handling.

@l./Source/cmDependsFortran.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDependsFortran.cxx.body:
The file implements the Fortran dependency resolver used by CMake.  
It scans Fortran source files, parses their include directives, gathers the modules required, and writes the makefile rules that enforce those dependencies.  
The code also supplies helper routines for locating module files in the include path, handling module stamping and copying, and for comparing module files to decide whether a rebuild is required.

@l./Source/cmDependsFortran.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDependsFortran.h.body: The header declares a Fortran‑dependency scanner that inherits from cmDepends. It offers helpers for copying .mod files, comparing stamp files, and a set of routines that locate required modules and emit dependency listings. Internally it keeps a unique_ptr to its implementation details.

@l./Source/cmDependsJava.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDependsJava.cxx.body:
The file implements a minimal dependency‑scanner class used by the cmake toolchain.  
The constructor and destructor are defaulted; the core routine `WriteDependencies` accepts a set of source file names and two output streams. It immediately verifies that at least one source is supplied, otherwise reports an error via `cmSystemTools::Error` and returns `false`. When called with a valid source, it simply writes nothing and returns `true`. The companion `CheckDependencies` method accepts an input stream and a filename but presently performs no validation logic, always returning `true`. The implementation is a placeholder that outlines where real dependency analysis would be plugged in.

@l./Source/cmDependsJava.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDependsJava.h.body:
The header declares a class that scans Java class files for dependencies.  
The class inherits from `cmDepends` and overrides the two pure virtual methods: `WriteDependencies` and `CheckDependencies`.  
It expects the constructor to receive the build‑directory name and the relative path from that directory to the target file, storing them for later use.  
The implementation relies on standard C++ containers (`std::set<std::string>`) and string/stream handling.

@l./Source/cmDependsJavaParserHelper.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDependsJavaParserHelper.cxx.body:
The helper encapsulates a small in‑memory parser that walks a Java source string, records every class it encounters, and produces one “.class” file name per class.  
When a new class is encountered it pushes a `CurrentClass` node onto an internal stack, and when the class ends it pops the node, attaching it to its parent’s `NestedClasses`.  
During parsing each identifier the helper keeps two lists: `ClassesFound` (the classes actually referenced) and `PackagesImport` (the imported packages). After a parse finishes it prints the collected information – current package, imported packages, and all discovered classes – to standard output and writes the file names that would be generated.  
All dynamically allocated strings are stored in a `std::unique_ptr` container so that `CleanupParser()` simply clears the vector, freeing every string.  
The public interface consists mainly of `ParseString()`/`ParseFile()` for running a parse, and the helper utilities `AddClassFound()` and `AddPackagesImport()` for adding entries.

@l./Source/cmDependsJavaParserHelper.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDependsJavaParserHelper.h.body: cmDependsJavaParserHelper.h implements a helper class that parses Java source files, tracks nested classes, collects used imports and class names, and manages current package and combine state.

@l./Source/cmDocumentation.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDocumentation.cxx.body: The file implements a command‑line help system for CMake. It parses arguments such as `--help‑…` or `--help‑full` and records the requested help items. When a request is found, the code searches the Help directory for matching “.rst” files, loads the first line of each, and outputs the help text in plain‑text or formatted sections. It also contains a tiny string‑normaliser that replaces legacy language tokens (e.g. LANG, CONFIG) in help keywords. The core functions coordinate printing of usage, individual command, module, policy, property or variable help, plus listings for each category. The implementation uses a small formatter class to render the collected sections to the supplied output stream.

@l./Source/cmDocumentation.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDocumentation.h.body:
`cmDocumentation.h` defines a small framework for generating and printing command‑line help for tools such as **cmake**, **CTest** and **CPack**.  
The `cmDocumentation` class parses the program’s arguments (`CheckOptions`), stores requested help requests, and emits the appropriate help text (`PrintRequestedDocumentation` → `PrintDocumentation`). It organizes help into named sections via `cmDocumentationSection` objects, supports adding a variety of standard sections (e.g., *Standard*, *CMake*, *CTest*, *CPack*), and offers facilities for appending or prepending custom entries.  The design relies on a formatter object (`cmDocumentationFormatter`) for formatting, and includes helper routines (`WarnFormFromFilename`, `GeneralizeKeyword`) that tidy up filenames or keywords for display.

@l./Source/cmDocumentationEntry.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDocumentationEntry.h.body: The file defines a lightweight struct for holding a documentation entry, storing a name string, a brief description string, and an optional custom prefix character. It guards the constructor with a preprocessor check on the C++ standard version, ensuring the constructor is only enabled when compiling under older C++ versions (≤ C++11). The struct members are default‑initialized to empty strings or a space character and are intentionally minimal to keep downstream consumers of this file simple and fast.

@l./Source/cmDocumentationFormatter.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmDocumentationFormatter.cxx.body: The source implements a formatter that emits documentation text in a column‑wrapped format. It splits input into words, buffering words in one of two buffers—one for normal text and one for pre‑formatted lines. When a space is seen it flushes the buffer of the other type, writes the accumulated words, and clears the buffer.
