@l./Source/cmJSONState.cxx.body: The implementation manages a JSON document’s state: it loads the whole file into an internal string, parses it with a custom reader into a `Json::Value` tree, and keeps a stack of key/value pairs representing the current parse path. Errors are stored with optional line‑column context computed from offsets, allowing callers to fetch the current key, the next key/value in the path, or a textual snippet of the surrounding JSON line for diagnostics. The class supplies helpers to push/pop context, retrieve the current key or the following key/value, and build context strings for error reporting.

@l./Source/cmJSONState.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmJSONState.h.body: cmJSONState is a utility for a JSON parser that records parsing errors and the context in which they were detected. It holds a stack of key/value pairs that represents the current path in the JSON tree, and records errors that occur while walking that path. Errors are stored with a line/column location and a message; the nested Error class formats this information for reporting. The class exposes helpers to add an error at a given offset or value, retrieve the accumulated error messages, and walk the current key stack (via push_stack / pop_stack). It also provides helpers to locate a line/column in the source text and extract a short snippet of the surrounding JSON for contextual error messages.

@l./Source/cmLDConfigLDConfigTool.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLDConfigLDConfigTool.cxx.body: The file implements a helper that, given a `cmRuntimeDependencyArchive`, runs the system’s `ldconfig` binary (located via `cmSystemTools::FindProgram`) with `-v -N -X` to list the library search paths. The output lines are parsed with a simple regular‑expression that extracts the value after a colon, and those values are pushed into a `std::vector<std::string>` that is returned to the caller. If any step fails—searching the binary, spawning the process, reading its output, or parsing the output—an error is recorded on the archive.

@l./Source/cmLDConfigLDConfigTool.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLDConfigLDConfigTool.h.body:
The header defines a concrete implementation of the generic LD‑config tool.  
Its constructor receives a pointer to a `cmRuntimeDependencyArchive`, which the instance uses to locate the configuration files at runtime.  
The sole virtual routine it implements, `GetLDConfigPaths`, fills a supplied vector with the absolute paths of all LD‑config files discovered in the archive. The class inherits from `cmLDConfigTool` and relies on the base class’s infrastructure for path resolution.

@l./Source/cmLDConfigTool.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLDConfigTool.cxx.body: The file implements a small helper class that keeps a reference to a `cmRuntimeDependencyArchive`. Its constructor simply stores the passed‑in pointer; no other logic is shown in the snippet. The rest of the file (outside the snippet) would contain the usual member functions that operate on that archive.

@l./Source/cmLDConfigTool.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLDConfigTool.h.body:
The header declares a helper class that wraps a pointer to a `cmRuntimeDependencyArchive`.  
Its sole public interface is a constructor accepting that archive, a defaulted virtual destructor, and a pure‑virtual `GetLDConfigPaths` that fills a supplied `std::vector<std::string>` with paths and returns a `bool` to signal success.  
The protected member simply holds the archive pointer; no other members are exposed.

@l./Source/cmLinkDirectoriesCommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLinkDirectoriesCommand.cxx.body: The file implements a `cmLinkDirectoriesCommand` command that parses its arguments to determine whether the new directories should be added before or after the existing ones. It normalizes each path (converting slashes, checking for full paths or generator expressions), applies the CMP0015 policy to decide whether a relative path should be made absolute, and finally appends the resolved directories to the makefile’s link‑directory list.

@l./Source/cmLinkDirectoriesCommand.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLinkDirectoriesCommand.h.body: The file defines the public interface for the *link‑directories* command. It declares a function that takes a vector of string arguments and a reference to a `cmExecutionStatus` object; the function populates the status and returns `true` only when the linking succeeds, otherwise `false`. The function is used in several parts of the code‑base to drive the directory linking logic.

@l./Source/cmLinkItem.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLinkItem.cxx.body:
Constructors build objects either from a name string or a target pointer, storing the cross‑flag and back‑trace.  
`AsStr()` returns the stored name if no target is set, otherwise it forwards the target’s name.  
Ordering (`operator<`) sorts first by target presence, then by target identity, then by the cross flag, and finally by the stored string.  
Equality (`operator==`) compares target pointer, string, and cross flag.  
`operator<<` streams the string returned by `AsStr()`.  
The derived `cmLinkImplItem` simply forwards to `cmLinkItem` and adds an extra flag (`CheckCMP0027`).

@l./Source/cmLinkItem.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLinkItem.h.body:
The file defines a hierarchy of classes and structs that model the various elements of a build target’s linking configuration.  
Core classes such as `cmLinkItem` and `cmLinkImplItem` represent individual object files or libraries, while structs like `cmLinkImplementationLibraries`, `cmLinkInterface`, `cmOptionalLinkInterface`, and `cmHeadToLinkInterfaceMap` capture the composition of direct dependencies, interface libraries, and context‑sensitive linking rules.  
A small helper function `CMP0003_ComputeLinkType` determines whether a given configuration should use a normal or debug link type, based on a list of known debug configurations.

@l./Source/cmLinkItemGraphVisitor.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLinkItemGraphVisitor.cxx.body: The implementation performs a depth‑first traversal of a link graph. It records which `cmLinkItem` objects have already been processed so that each node is visited only once, and it also records links between items to avoid repeating the same dependency twice. As it walks the graph it calls `OnItem` for each node, then triggers `OnDirectLink` when it encounters a link of a particular type. When a link is indirect relative to the original root, it fires `OnIndirectLink`. The helper `GetDependencies` pulls the dependency data from a target’s implementation, interface, object and utility libraries, building a map that the visitor iterates over. The code is deliberately straightforward, keeping the public API minimal while allowing callers to hook in custom behaviour via the virtual callbacks.

@l./Source/cmLinkItemGraphVisitor.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLinkItemGraphVisitor.h.body:
The header declares an abstract visitor class that walks a graph of linked cmLinkItem objects.  
It supplies a public entry point (`VisitGraph`) and a helper (`VisitItem`) that invokes protected callbacks (`OnItem`, `OnDirectLink`, `OnIndirectLink`) so derived visitors can implement custom logic.  
Internally it tracks already‑visited items and links in `VisitedItems` and `VisitedLinks` to guarantee each node and each edge is processed at most once, even when cycles exist.  
A small static helper (`GetDependencies`) gathers the dependency map for a given target and configuration, used by the traversal routine.

@l./Source/cmLinkLibrariesCommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLinkLibrariesCommand.cxx.body:
The implementation parses a list of library identifiers supplied as command‑line arguments.  
When it encounters the special prefixes “debug” or “optimized”, it consumes the following argument as the library name and records the corresponding property in the makefile.  
Finally, every valid library name is appended to the `LINK_LIBRARIES` property, and the function reports success or an error through the `status` object.

@l./Source/cmLinkLibrariesCommand.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLinkLibrariesCommand.h.body:
`cmLinkLibrariesCommand` is a thin wrapper that initiates a linking step.  
- It takes a **vector of string arguments** – typically `-l<lib>` flags or plain library names – and a reference to a `cmExecutionStatus` object that will receive the outcome of the command.  
- On invocation it forwards the arguments to the underlying build system, populates `status` with the result, and returns **true** on success or **false** on failure.  
- The header pulls in the minimal dependencies (`string`, `vector`) and the project‑specific `cmConfigure.h`, exposing only this simple interface for callers.

@l./Source/cmLinkLineComputer.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLinkLineComputer.cxx.body: The file implements the `cmLinkLineComputer` class, which builds the command‑line arguments needed for a linker. It holds flags that determine whether responses, Ninja multi‑output, or Watcom quoting are used. The key public methods collect linker flags: `ComputeLinkLibs`, `ComputeLinkPath`, `ComputeRPath`, and `ComputeFrameworkPath`. Internally it relies on a `cmOutputConverter` to escape and format strings for shells or responses, and it appends the constructed strings into a `cmComputeLinkInformation` instance via `AppendValues`. The class provides setters (`SetUseWatcomQuote`, `SetUseNinjaMulti`, etc.) to switch behaviour for different build‑system back‑ends.

@l./Source/cmLinkLineComputer.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLinkLineComputer.h.body: The header implements a helper that, given a `cmComputeLinkInformation` instance and a target platform, calculates the proper linker arguments. It walks through the various build‑system switches (Watcom quoting, Ninja‑multi‑link, relink) and produces the fully‑qualified path strings for libraries, frameworks and the RPATH. The public interface exposes the conversion helpers and the core `ComputeLinkPath/ComputeFrameworkPath` helpers that build the final “–l …” or “-framework …” fragments used by a generator target.

@l./Source/cmLinkLineDeviceComputer.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLinkLineDeviceComputer.cxx.body: This file implements a helper class that decides whether a CUDA target needs a device‑link step. It examines the target’s linked libraries, filters out shared libraries and framework entries, and builds the list of libraries that should be passed to the device linker. The helper queries properties such as CUDA_RESOLVE_DEVICE_SYMBOLS and CUDA_SEPARABLE_COMPILATION to decide when device linking is required, and supplies this information to the rest of the build system.

@l./Source/cmLinkLineDeviceComputer.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLinkLineDeviceComputer.h.body:
The header declares a `cmLinkLineDeviceComputer` type that derives from `cmLinkLineComputer`.  
Its constructor stores an `cmOutputConverter*` and a reference to a `cmStateDirectory`.  
The class implements three main responsibilities:  

1. **Decision logic** – `ComputeRequiresDeviceLinking()` and its variant `ComputeRequiresDeviceLinkingIPOFlag()` examine a `cmComputeLinkInformation` object to determine whether a device‑specific link step is required.  

2. **Link library handling** – `ComputeLinkLibraries()` produces the list of libraries to be linked for a target, appending the proper strings to a supplied vector.  

3. **Linker configuration** – `GetLinkerLanguage()` returns the name of the linker tool that should be invoked for a specific generator target, based on the supplied configuration string.  

The helper function `requireDeviceLinking()` is a free function used by other modules to test a target‑generator pair against a configuration string.

@l./Source/cmLinkedTree.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLinkedTree.h.body:
`cmLinkedTree` stores nodes in a `std::vector`.  
Each node knows the position of its parent via the `UpPositions` vector.  
The `iterator` class keeps a tree pointer and an index; incrementing it follows the parent chain.  
`Push` appends a new element after a given iterator and returns an iterator for that element.  
`Pop` removes a node and, if it was the last child, trims the trailing storage.  
`Truncate` prunes the tree to keep only the root and its immediate child.  
The class is designed mainly to support the `cmState` logic, not a generic container adaptor.

@l./Source/cmList.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmList.cxx.body: The file implements a custom string list class that supports advanced manipulation: filtering by regex or inclusion mode, sorting with various comparison strategies (file‑basename, natural order, case sensitivity), and a flexible transform system that can apply actions such as append, prepend, case conversion, stripping, or regex‑based replacement. It also provides helper classes for selecting specific elements (by index, range, or regular expression) and utilities for computing and inserting items while correctly handling nested separators and escaped semicolons.

@l./Source/cmList.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmList.h.body:
**cmList – concise overview** | Item | What it does | |-------|--------------| | **Purpose** | A thin wrapper around a string list that keeps entries delimited by a `';'` separator. It is used wherever a CMake‑style list of values is required (e.g. CMake variable lists). | | **Construction** | • **Default** – creates an empty list.
• **From string** – parses a semi‑colon‑separated string into the internal vector.
• **From an array** – accepts an initializer‑list or a `std::vector` directly. | | **Assignment / copying** | The class offers `assign()` to replace the current list with the contents of another `cmList`. A copy‑constructor and assignment operator are also provided. | | **Joining / Splitting** | • `join()` – concatenates the internal elements back into a single string.
• `split()` – static helper that breaks a given string into a `cmList` by the same delimiter. | | **Insertion / Removal** | • `insert()` – inserts a string at an arbitrary position.
• `remove()` – drops an element at a given index. | | **Transformations** | • `transform()` – passes a supplied `cmFunction` (or a functor) to each element, returning a new list of the results.
• `transformFirst()` – does the same but stops after the first element that satisfies a condition. | | **Utilities** | • `toString()` – returns the raw delimiter‑separated string.
• `asArray()` – returns a `std::vector` of the current contents. | | **Notable helpers** | • Static helpers such as `cmList::join()` and `cmList::split()` are used throughout the CMake codebase to normalise list handling. | **Key take‑away** - `cmList` is a reusable helper for any code that needs a semi‑colon separated list of string values. - It supplies the usual container operations (copy, assign, insert, remove) plus string‑specific helpers (`join`, `split`). - All operations are performed on an internal `std::vector`; conversion helpers keep the implementation simple and efficient.

@l./Source/cmListCommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmListCommand.cxx.body: The file implements the core list‑based sub‑commands for the **cmake** language. It provides a single entry point, `cmListCommand`, that receives a vector of arguments and dispatches to a small set of handlers defined in a static dispatch table. Each handler implements a specific list operation—such as creating, appending, pre‑appending, retrieving an element, removing elements, filtering, sorting, or transforming a list—using the helper routines in the file (`GetIndexArg`, `GetListString`, `GetList`). Policy checks guard behaviour (e.g. warnings, old or new behaviours) and they report errors via the `cmExecutionStatus` object. The code is the glue that translates user‑supplied list sub‑commands into concrete `cmList` manipulations.

@l./Source/cmListCommand.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmListCommand.h.body: The file declares a single helper: a `cmListCommand` function that takes a collection of string arguments and a reference to a status object, returning `true` on success. The header pulls in the project‑wide configuration header, pulls in standard containers, and relies on a forward declaration of `cmExecutionStatus`. It is meant to be called from various parts of the code that need to perform a list‑style operation and report the outcome through the status object.

@l./Source/cmListFileCache.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmListFileCache.cxx.body: The implementation parses custom list‑file scripts, tokenizing the input through a lexer, collecting function definitions, and ensuring proper nesting of flow‑control blocks. It records context via a back‑trace stack for error reporting, and uses a messenger to surface fatal errors. The code includes utilities for expanding list arguments and formatting context for diagnostics.

@l./Source/cmListFileCache.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmListFileCache.h.body: The header defines small helper types and wrappers for handling parsed list files in the cmake system. It contains a cache class that stores functions parsed from list files, structures that describe a function’s name, line range, and its arguments, and lightweight templates (`BT`/`BTs`) that tag values with a back‑trace for ordering and equality checks. The file also supplies parsing helpers that read a list file or string into a vector of these function descriptors.

@l./Source/cmListFileLexer.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmListFileLexer.h.body:
The header declares a lexer for parsing list‑file syntax. It supplies a token enum for whitespace, identifiers, argument delimiters (quoted, bracketed, unquoted), brackets, comments, and error tokens, a token struct storing the type, text and source‑position, and a BOM enum.  

The API provides functions to create a lexer, configure it with a file name or string, perform lexical scanning, query current line/column, obtain token text, and clean up.

@l./Source/cmLoadCacheCommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLoadCacheCommand.cxx.body: The file implements the `load_cache` command used by the CMake tool. It processes arguments that may request a special `READ_WITH_PREFIX` form, validates the supplied cache file, parses its lines, and imports named entries into the current makefile while optionally applying a prefix and filtering by explicit include/exclude lists. Its logic walks through the provided arguments, separates internal‑from external cache elements, and finally registers the selected variables in the makefile’s definition table.

@l./Source/cmLoadCacheCommand.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLoadCacheCommand.h.body: The header declares a helper that parses a vector of command‑line arguments, creates a cache‑load command for the **cmake** build system, and returns a boolean indicating success. It supplies the result status through the `cmExecutionStatus` reference and relies on the public `cmConfigure.h` interface for required constants and utilities.

@l./Source/cmLoadCommandCommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLoadCommandCommand.cxx.body: cmLoadCommandCommand.cxx implements the runtime loading of CMake command plugins. It defines a signal‑handler guard to catch crashes, wraps the plugin entry point in a LoadedCommandImpl, and registers the command in the CMake state once its init function is located. The file orchestrates discovery of the shared module, loading it, retrieving the init symbol, and attaching the command to the makefile’s execution context while handling errors and cleanup.

@l./Source/cmLocalCommonGenerator.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLocalCommonGenerator.cxx.body: This file implements the local generator that knows how to set up Fortran‑specific compiler flags and how to determine output file names for compiled objects. The constructor simply pulls the list of generator‑specific configuration names from the makefile. `GetWorkingDirectory()` returns the current binary directory that the state snapshot points to. `GetTargetFortranFlags()` builds a string of flags by pulling the appropriate module‑output and module‑directory definitions from the makefile, converting them to shell‑escaped form, and appending the resulting flags to the output string. `ComputeObjectFilenames()` iterates over a map of source files and applies the target’s custom object extension (if any) to produce the final object file names.

@l./Source/cmLocalCommonGenerator.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLocalCommonGenerator.h.body: `cmLocalCommonGenerator` is a thin wrapper around a local generator that exposes a handful of helper routines for the build‑system core. It keeps a list of configuration names that are available for the current target and offers a public accessor that other generators can query.  The class implements two virtual hooks: `GetWorkingDirectory()` and `GetTargetFortranFlags()`, both of which are expected to be overridden by concrete generator types.  It also supplies the implementation of `ComputeObjectFilenames()`, a routine that walks a collection of source files and produces corresponding object file paths in a shared mapping table.  The constructor hooks the global generator and the associated makefile instance, while the destructor cleans up any allocated resources.  Finally, the `friend` declaration exposes certain internals of `cmCommonTargetGenerator` to this class, enabling tight collaboration between the two generator families.

@l./Source/cmLocalGenerator.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLocalGenerator.cxx.body: The source file implements the core logic for generating Makefile rules in CMake. It defines a single class that orchestrates the creation of target and output rules, handling custom and utility commands, and applies compiler‑specific flag handling (shared/static, visibility, inline, etc.). It contains helper routines for handling PCH files, PCH dependencies, and ensuring that generated object names stay within filesystem limits. The generator also tracks various include‑search paths, flag collections, and the mapping of source files to output artifacts. The implementation is organized into several helper blocks: command addition helpers, flag assembly, dependency resolution, and rule‑generation utilities. The file is heavily focused on producing coherent, portable build rules while maintaining an internal cache of computed paths and flags for efficiency.

@l./Source/cmLocalGenerator.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLocalGenerator.h.body: `cmLocalGenerator` is an abstract base that a global generator creates to emit the actual build‑system files for a single source‑root.  It owns the logic for figuring out compiler and linker flags, collecting source‑level includes, by‑products, and custom command hooks, and then writes the final makefile, install rules, and test files for that generator’s tree.  The class also exposes helper routines for handling target‑specific flags, dependency tracking, and Unity/IPC support, and is the common entry point for all concrete generator subclasses.

@l./Source/cmLocalGhsMultiGenerator.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLocalGhsMultiGenerator.cxx.body: The class implements a local GNU‑make‑style generator that emits separate build targets for each source file. It walks through the targets in build‑order, invokes a GHS‑specific target generator for each, and guarantees unique object file names by detecting name collisions and re‑suffixing them when necessary.

@l./Source/cmLocalGhsMultiGenerator.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLocalGhsMultiGenerator.h.body: The header declares a concrete generator that produces a separate .gpj file for each target in a mirrored directory. It inherits from cmLocalGenerator, stores a pointer to a global generator and the makefile, and implements the key hooks: Generate() to emit the makefile contents, GetTargetDirectory() to resolve the target’s output path, and ComputeObjectFilenames() to build the source‑to‑object mapping for the target.

@l./Source/cmLocalNinjaGenerator.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLocalNinjaGenerator.cxx.body: The file implements the local Ninja generator used by CMake to emit a `build.ninja` file for a given generator configuration. It builds the output‑directory layout, writes the common and per‑config generators, and emits the top‑level header that declares the Ninja version, working directory, and includes of auxiliary files. It handles multi‑configuration builds by iterating over each configuration, creating per‑config “impl” files and writing the appropriate include blocks. The generator also creates and writes custom command targets, handling both the simple and cross‑configuration scenarios. For each custom command it expands the rule placeholders, expands the command line (including handling of long commands via shell scripts on Windows), writes the command line to Ninja, and writes the depfile handling. Finally, it registers any additional “clean” files that must be removed when cleaning. The code also writes the pool definitions derived from the `JOB_POOLS` property, and emits the description comment for the build file.

@l./Source/cmLocalNinjaGenerator.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLocalNinjaGenerator.h.body:
The header declares a helper class that writes a local *build.ninja* file.  
It derives from the common ninja generator, keeps track of the working directory, and exposes utilities for composing command lines, appending target outputs, and producing the dependency file for each target.  
Internally it stores a map of custom‑command objects to the targets that invoke them, and builds the various sections of the ninja configuration (header, pools, rules, etc.) that the generator emits.

@l./Source/cmLocalUnixMakefileGenerator3.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLocalUnixMakefileGenerator3.body: The source implements a Unix‑specific makefile generator that writes rules, resolves relative paths to full ones, scans for dependencies, and outputs custom commands and clean targets while handling quoted paths.

@l./Source/cmLocalUnixMakefileGenerator3.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLocalUnixMakefileGenerator3.body: The `cmLocalUnixMakefileGenerator3` class produces the Unix‑style makefiles used by CMake. It writes rule files, handles implicit and explicit dependencies, and writes the supporting variables and convenience rules needed to build targets. It also provides helpers for quoting paths, escaping commands, and creating the special “clean” or “test” rules that the tool uses at run‑time.

@l./Source/cmLocale.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmLocale.h.body: A small RAII guard that stores the current locale on construction, switches to the C locale, and restores the original locale in the destructor. The copy/move operators are deleted to avoid double‑restore side‑effects.

@l./Source/cmMSVC60LinkLineComputer.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMSVC60LinkLineComputer.cxx.body: The file implements a specialized link‑reference converter that patches a known issue in MSVC 6.0: when a library file contains spaces, the standard parser mis‑interprets the path. The implementation detects the last space in the supplied path, truncates the string up to that point, expands any short‑name segment to a short‑path form (using `cmSystemTools::GetShortPath`) and then re‑appends the remaining part of the path that contains no spaces. If this transformation fails, the routine falls back to the base class logic for normal conversion.

@l./Source/cmMSVC60LinkLineComputer.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMSVC60LinkLineComputer.h.body: The header defines a concrete subclass of cmLinkLineComputer that holds a pointer to an output‑converter and a reference to a state directory. Its only responsibility is to override ConvertToLinkReference, translating a plain input string into the correctly‑formatted link string expected by MSVC 60.

@l./Source/cmMacroCommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMacroCommand.cxx.body: The file implements the logic that executes a macro command in the CMake engine. It defines a helper class (`cmMacroHelperCommand`) that, when invoked, expands the macro’s arguments, verifies the required number of arguments, sets up a macro scope, substitutes formal parameters with actual values (including `${ARGC}`, `${ARGN}`, `${ARGV}`), and then runs the list of stored functions for the macro. It also implements a blocker (`cmMacroFunctionBlocker`) that records the macro definition (name and arguments) and later replays it by creating a `cmMacroHelperCommand` instance and adding it to the execution state. The code handles errors, nested errors, return and break control flow, and interacts with the `cmMakefile` and `cmExecutionStatus` objects to coordinate the macro’s execution.

@l./Source/cmMacroCommand.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMacroCommand.h.body: The header introduces a single helper function that accepts a list of arguments and a status object, runs a macro‑style command, and reports success by returning a bool. It pulls in the standard string/vector types and a configuration header to wire the command into the larger engine, and is the entry point used by other modules to invoke macro blocks.

@l./Source/cmMakeDirectoryCommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMakeDirectoryCommand.cxx.body: The function `cmMakeDirectoryCommand` validates that exactly one path argument is supplied, ensures that the given directory can be written into the current source tree via `CanIWriteThisFile`, records an error and marks a fatal error if the permission check fails, and finally delegates the actual creation to `cmSystemTools::MakeDirectory`.

@l./Source/cmMakeDirectoryCommand.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMakeDirectoryCommand.h.body: The header declares a single helper function that registers a list of source directories to the build system. The function receives a vector of directory strings and a status object to report success or failure. It returns `true` when the directories are accepted and scheduled for building; otherwise it reports an error via the `cmExecutionStatus` object. The command is used to set up “auxiliary” source directories that will be built without recursive processing, while ensuring that a matching sub‑directory is created in the output tree.

@l./Source/cmMakefile.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMakefile.cxx.body: The file implements the core engine of CMake: it parses list‑files, manages scopes and policies, defines and registers targets, handles custom commands and utilities, and orchestrates the generation of the final makefiles while tracking state, variables, and errors throughout the build process.

@l./Source/cmMakefile.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMakefile.h.body: The `cmMakefile` class is the core engine that parses a CMakeLists.txt file, expands variables, and builds an in‑memory representation of the project. It keeps track of defined variables, target objects, and dependency trees. It offers APIs for adding custom commands, utilities, libraries, and alias targets, and for configuring include directories, compile and link options, and system include flags. The class also manages policy scopes and scopes for functions, macros and loops, as well as the stack of deferred commands. On top‑level it orchestrates the generation step that emits the final makefile and registers build‑time installers and test generators.

@l./Source/cmMakefileExecutableTargetGen.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMakefileExecutableTargetGen.body: This source implements the generation of Makefile rules for building executable targets. It orchestrates the creation of device‑specific link scripts (CUDA/Clang), handles pre‑build/pre‑link custom commands, and constructs the final link command by expanding rule placeholders with language‑specific flags and libraries. The code also supports device‑enabled linking, relinking logic for installed binaries, and manages the cleanup of intermediate artifacts and symlinks for each target.

@l./Source/cmMakefileExecutableTargetGen.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMakefileExecutableTargetGen.body: The class implements a make‑file target generator that knows how to generate build rules for an executable target. It inherits from cmMakefileTargetGenerator, storing the target in its constructor and overriding WriteRuleFiles to emit the appropriate Make rules. The protected virtual helpers— WriteExecutableRule, WriteDeviceExecutableRule, and WriteNvidiaDeviceExecutableRule—are hooks for producing rules for standard, device‑agnostic, and NVIDIA‑device executables respectively, and the private DeviceLinkObject string holds the intermediate link command string used during the rule generation.

@l./Source/cmMakefileLibraryTargetGenera.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMakefileLibraryTargetGenera.body: The implementation drives the generation of make‑file rules for library targets in the CMake Unix backend. It assembles the appropriate link, device‑link, and response‑file rules for each library type (static, shared, module, object, frameworks) and emits the required clean and symlink rules for the resulting files. It relies on helper classes to build the command lists, expand placeholders, and emit the driver rules that tie all pieces together.

@l./Source/cmMakefileLibraryTargetGenera.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMakefileLibraryTargetGenera.body:
The header declares a concrete subclass of **`cmMakefileTargetGenerator`** that implements the rule‑generation logic for library build targets.  
Key responsibilities:

- Stores a pointer to the owning target in the constructor.  
- Overrides the virtual `~cmMakefileTargetGenerator()` destructor.  
- Implements `WriteRuleFiles()` – the entry point invoked by the build system to emit Makefile rules.  
- Provides helper functions that emit specific rules for:  
  • object‑only libraries,  
  • static libraries,  
  • shared libraries (optionally relinking),  
  • module libraries,  
  • device‑linked libraries, and  
  • NVIDIA‑device‑linked libraries (taking a rule variable and command list).  
- Holds the framework version string for macOS‑X framework support.  
- Keeps an internal string `DeviceLinkObject` used when writing device rules.

@l./Source/cmMakefileProfilingData.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMakefileProfilingData.cxx.body: The file implements a simple JSON‑based profiler that writes “begin” (B) and “end” (E) events to a file. It opens the file on construction, writes a JSON array start (`[`), appends events with timestamps and optional arguments, and closes with a `]`. A small RAII helper (`RAII`) automatically emits a stop event when it goes out of scope. The code uses chrono to stamp events and a `Json::StreamWriter` to serialize the data.

@l./Source/cmMakefileProfilingData.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMakefileProfilingData.h.body:
`cmMakefileProfilingData` is a thin wrapper that records profiling ticks.  
When constructed it opens a file stream and owns a `Json::StreamWriter`.  
`StartEntry` snapshots a timestamp and a named event (optionally with arguments) and writes it in JSON format to the stream; `StopEntry` closes the record.  
The nested `RAII` helper turns an RAII‑style guard into a scoped entry marker that automatically calls `StopEntry` when it goes out of scope.

@l./Source/cmMakefileTargetGenerator.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMakefileTargetGenerator.cxx.body: The file defines the **cmMakefileTargetGenerator** class, which walks through a set of source objects and emits the requisite Makefile fragments for building them—handling pre‑processing, assembly, and linking for multiple toolchains, and wiring response files, link scripts, and custom commands while aggregating the resulting variable lists.

@l./Source/cmMakefileTargetGenerator.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMakefileTargetGenerator.h.body: The class implements the code‑generation part of CMake for Unix makefiles. It emits a target‑specific rule file, writes object‑ and dependency rules, emits progress‑tracking hooks, and drives the build of both ordinary and CUDA‑linked objects. It also emits the device‑link rule for the device compiler, emits custom‑command wrappers, handles response files, and finalises the list of objects to be built or cleaned, while wiring up both local and global generators for the target.

@l./Source/cmMakefileUtilityTargetGenera.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMakefileUtilityTargetGenera.body: The implementation provides the logic for generating a utility‑target makefile. It creates the rule file, writes the necessary include directives, emits the custom‑command rules (pre‑/post‑build), and finally emits the driver, clean, and dependency rules that tie the target’s outputs into the build graph.

@l./Source/cmMakefileUtilityTargetGenera.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMakefileUtilityTargetGenera.body: The header declares a class that, when constructed with a target, is responsible for writing the make‑file rules that correspond to that target. It inherits from the generic target‑generator base, holds a reference to the supplied `cmGeneratorTarget`, and implements the core `WriteRuleFiles()` routine that emits the makefile entries for that target.

@l./Source/cmMarkAsAdvancedCommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMarkAsAdvancedCommand.cxx.body: The routine parses command‑line arguments that request marking of a cache entry as “advanced.” It walks through each variable name, consults the current CMP0102 policy state, optionally emits a warning if the entry is missing, and finally sets (or resets) the “ADVANCED” property to the requested value, handling the special “CLEAR”/“FORCE” override cases that force an overwrite of the existing flag.

@l./Source/cmMarkAsAdvancedCommand.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMarkAsAdvancedCommand.h.body: The header declares the `cmMarkAsAdvancedCommand` function, which registers a CMake command as “advanced” by passing its arguments to the underlying registry. It pulls in the core configuration and status types (`cmConfigure.h`, `cmExecutionStatus`), and provides the thin wrapper that other modules call to signal that a command should be treated specially during parsing.

@l./Source/cmMathCommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMathCommand.cxx.body: The code implements a command‑handling routine for the “cmake” tool. It validates arguments for the `EXPR` sub‑command, supports output in decimal or hexadecimal format, and stores the computed value in a makefile definition. Errors are reported via the `cmExecutionStatus` object, and warnings from the expression parser are logged through the makefile’s message system.

@l./Source/cmMathCommand.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMathCommand.h.body: The header declares the core interface for the math‑command subsystem. It pulls in the build‑time configuration header, and pulls in the standard library types needed to represent argument tokens (`std::vector<std::string>`). A small helper class, `cmExecutionStatus`, is defined to carry back any error or completion information. The key function, `cmMathCommand`, is declared to take a list of string arguments, process them as a mathematical expression (details handled elsewhere), and return a boolean flag indicating success while writing any status information into the supplied `cmExecutionStatus` reference.

@l./Source/cmMessageCommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMessageCommand.cxx.body: The file implements the core message‑handling routine for CMake. It defines an enum for check states, helpers to prepend contextual text to messages, and a main function that parses message arguments to decide log level, message type (error, warning, notice, etc.), and dispatches the message either to the messenger, status output, or a log file when enabled. It also handles special cases such as `CHECK_START`, `CHECK_PASS`, `CHECK_FAIL`, and deprecation handling.

@l./Source/cmMessageCommand.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMessageCommand.h.body: The header declares a single helper that accepts a list of strings and a status object, emits the concatenated strings as a user‑visible message, and reports success via its bool return and fills the status reference with any error information.

@l./Source/cmMessageMetadata.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMessageMetadata.h.body: cmMessageMetadata.h declares a small helper structure that bundles the title string and terminal‑color code that other modules use to format console output consistently. The structure holds a C‑string pointer for the title and an integer flag defaulting to the normal terminal color. The header pulls in the terminal system so that any source file that needs to emit a message can simply populate this struct and hand it to the output routine.

@l./Source/cmMessageType.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMessageType.h.body: The header declares an enum `MessageType` that categorizes severity levels used throughout the project—ranging from generic messages to internal and fatal errors. Inside the `Message` namespace it defines a second enum, `LogLevel`, that further refines those categories into specific logging verbosity levels (error, warning, notice, status, verbose, debug, trace). These types are used by the logging infrastructure to tag and dispatch messages consistently across the codebase.

@l./Source/cmMessenger.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMessenger.cxx.body: The file implements CMake’s message handling logic: it converts developer‑level warnings/errors into the appropriate severity for output, determines whether a message should be shown (respecting user‑set suppression flags), and formats the final output string with a header, context stack, and optional stack trace for internal errors.  The code also hooks into an optional debugger adapter for additional diagnostics.

@l./Source/cmMessenger.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmMessenger.h.body: The header defines a messaging subsystem that manages the creation, presentation, and filtering of diagnostic messages. It supports message‑type conversion, optional backtrace inclusion, and two tiers of warning control (developer and deprecated warnings) that can be suppressed or treated as errors. When compiled with the debugging flag, an optional debugger adapter can be attached to drive debugger‑specific handling.

@l./Source/cmNewLineStyle.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmNewLineStyle.cxx.body: The file implements a small helper class that parses a command‑line option named `NEWLINE_STYLE` to select one of three newline styles (LF or CRLF) and a few aliases (UNIX, DOS, WIN32). It stores the chosen style as an enum value, offers `IsValid()` to confirm the value is set, `GetCharacters()` to return the corresponding string (`"\n"` or `"\r\n"`), and simple getters/setters. Invalid values are flagged with an empty string and an error message is produced when an unsupported style token is supplied.

@l./Source/cmNewLineStyle.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmNewLineStyle.h.body:
cmNewLineStyle.h defines a small utility class that encapsulates newline‑style handling.  
The class exposes an enum with the three possible line‑endings (invalid, LF, and CRLF), and offers setters/getters plus helpers for validating a chosen style, parsing a list of command‑line arguments for a newline specification, and retrieving the raw character sequence that represents the selected style. The implementation is intentionally lightweight and platform‑agnostic, making it suitable for embedding in larger configuration or build‑time parsing logic.

@l./Source/cmNinjaLinkLineComputer.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmNinjaLinkLineComputer.cxx.body: The source implements a small helper class that forwards conversion of a library name to a Ninja‑compatible path. The constructor simply stores a pointer to a global generator object; the overridden `ConvertToLinkReference` method then calls that generator’s `ConvertToNinjaPath`, passing along the library string and returning the resulting path string.

@l./Source/cmNinjaLinkLineComputer.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmNinjaLinkLineComputer.h.body: cmNinjaLinkLineComputer is a concrete implementation of cmLinkLineComputer that turns an arbitrary string into a Ninja‑style link reference. It depends on a cmOutputConverter for naming resolution, a cmStateDirectory for context, and a global generator instance for shared look‑ups. The constructor stores a pointer to the generator; ConvertToLinkReference takes a string and returns its resolved form, overriding the virtual interface.

@l./Source/cmNinjaLinkLineDeviceComputer.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmNinjaLinkLineDeviceComputer.body:
The implementation defines a concrete device‑computer that converts a library name into a Ninja‑style path.  
It inherits from `cmLinkLineDeviceComputer`, receives an `outputConverter`, a `stateDir`, and a pointer to a global Ninja generator (`gg`).  
In its constructor it simply stores the generator pointer (`GG`).  
The public helper `ConvertToLinkReference` forwards the library name to the stored generator’s `ConvertToNinjaPath` routine, returning the resulting string.

@l./Source/cmNinjaLinkLineDeviceComputer.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmNinjaLinkLineDeviceComputer.body: `cmNinjaLinkLineDeviceComputer` inherits from `cmLinkLineDeviceComputer` and implements the virtual `ConvertToLinkReference` method. Its constructor takes an output‑converter pointer, a reference to a state‑directory, and a pointer to a global ninja generator, which it stores privately. The class blocks copying and assignment for safety. All other parts of the project use this class to translate a given string into a link reference string via the overridden conversion routine.

@l./Source/cmNinjaNormalTargetGenerator..author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmNinjaNormalTargetGenerator..body: The source builds Ninja rules for ordinary build targets. It parses target configuration, emits link‑and‑device‑link commands, supports CUDA‑specific rules, and writes the resulting rule snippets to the appropriate output directories. It orchestrates a small number of lambda helpers and private utilities to construct rule strings and handle response‑file usage for linking.

@l./Source/cmNinjaNormalTargetGenerator..author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmNinjaNormalTargetGenerator..body: The class implements the logic for emitting standard “normal” build rules for a Ninja target. It drives the generation of language‑specific linker rules, writes device‑aware link and object rules, and computes the final command vectors that will be written into the Ninja build file.

@l./Source/cmNinjaTargetGenerator.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmNinjaTargetGenerator.cxx.body: The file implements the `cmNinjaTargetGenerator` class, which drives the construction of Ninja build files for CMake projects. It orchestrates scanning of source files, expands placeholders, produces Swift‑output mappings, and emits compile, scan, and dependency rules while managing cleanup of intermediate artifacts.

@l./Source/cmNinjaTargetGenerator.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmNinjaTargetGenerator.h.body: The header defines a class that drives the emission of Ninja‑style build rules for a given CMake target. It encapsulates the logic for computing compiler flags, include paths, and pre‑processing rules for every language; it emits the command lines that the Ninja executor will run. The class also records the objects, dependencies, and scanning information that must be written out, and it knows how to format file names and paths in a Ninja‑friendly form. Finally it supplies support for special cases such as Swift modules and macOS bundles.

@l./Source/cmNinjaTypes.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmNinjaTypes.h.body:
Defines the core data structures used by the ninja‑based build system in **cmake**.  
The header contains the following elements:

* An enum describing whether a target depends on artifacts or ordering.  
* Two convenient aliases (`cmNinjaDeps`, `cmNinjaVars`) for `std::vector<std::string>` and `std::map<std::string, std::string>`.  
* Two lightweight POD classes – `cmNinjaRule` and `cmNinjaBuild`.  
  * `cmNinjaRule` holds the name of a rule together with optional command, description, comment, dependency‑file paths, and flags such as `Generator`.  
  * `cmNinjaBuild` stores a rule name plus collections of outputs, implicit outputs, work‑dir outputs, dependencies (explicit, implicit, order‑only), and a map of variables.  

These types are employed elsewhere in the project to materialise ninja build files – the rules describe a single build step; a `cmNinjaBuild` instance represents an individual task.

@l./Source/cmNinjaUtilityTargetGenerator.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmNinjaUtilityTargetGenerator.body:
The class builds the Ninja build rules for a utility target.  
It gathers pre‑ and post‑build custom commands, resolves their outputs and dependencies, and writes the corresponding phony rule (including any clean‑up artifacts).  
When the target is per‑config it emits a rule per configuration, otherwise it falls back to the global rule; it also creates an alias so the logical target can be invoked from any directory.

@l./Source/cmNinjaUtilityTargetGenerator.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmNinjaUtilityTargetGenerator.body: The `cmNinjaUtilityTargetGenerator` class is a concrete implementation of the abstract `cmNinjaTargetGenerator` interface. It receives a `cmGeneratorTarget` object in its constructor and implements the `Generate` method, which writes Ninja build statements specific to a “utility” target. Internally, it calls the helper `WriteUtilBuildStatements` to serialize the provided configuration string and the target’s build‑file configuration into the Ninja file format expected by the Ninja build system. The class ensures resources are cleaned up in its destructor and follows the base class’ contract for generating build rules.

@l./Source/cmOSXBundleGenerator.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmOSXBundleGenerator.cxx.body: The file implements a helper class that, when invoked from the CMake build engine, creates the files‑ and directory layout expected by macOS‑X frameworks or applications. It wires together the generator target, local generator, and makefile objects to lay out the framework’s top‑level .framework bundle, populate the Resources/Headers/… sub‑folders, generate the Info.plist files, and create the required symbolic links (e.g., Current → version and version → current) that make the bundle discoverable at run‑time. The public API exposes CreateAppBundle, CreateFramework, CreateCFBundle and helper methods that drive the symlink creation and directory setup for the various “content” levels (content, full, and version directories).

@l./Source/cmOSXBundleGenerator.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmOSXBundleGenerator.h.body: The header declares a `cmOSXBundleGenerator` helper that orchestrates the creation of OS X‑style application bundles, frameworks and CF bundles. It accepts optional “skip parts” flags, produces the relevant content directories, and exposes a callback type for emitting content statements. Internally it keeps a reference to the target generator, a makefile helper and a set of content‑folder paths that it uses to populate the bundle.

@l./Source/cmOptionCommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmOptionCommand.cxx.body: The file implements the command that processes an option directive in CMake. It validates that the option name and help string are supplied (two or three arguments), checks the current policy state to decide whether to warn or silently ignore an already‑defined option, and then updates or creates the corresponding cache entry in the internal state, setting its value according to the supplied flag or default “Off”. If an existing definition conflicts with the new one, it removes the old snapshot entry before adding the new one and may emit a policy warning.

@l./Source/cmOptionCommand.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmOptionCommand.h.body: The header declares a helper that parses a vector of argument strings and reports the resulting run status via a `cmExecutionStatus` reference. The function returns a boolean flag indicating whether the option handling succeeded, and the calling code can inspect the status object afterwards. It pulls in the common `cmConfigure` definitions and hooks into the broader option‑handling framework.

@l./Source/cmOrderDirectories.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmOrderDirectories.cxx.body:
The file implements the runtime‑library ordering logic used by CMake.  
It defines a constraint hierarchy (`cmOrderDirectoriesConstraint` and its subclasses) that records a library’s directory and its soname, checks for file conflicts in a directory, and builds a graph of those conflicts.  
A top‑level `cmOrderDirectories` class walks that graph (DFS) to emit an ordering that satisfies all constraints, while reporting cycles or conflicting directories via the target’s generator.

@l./Source/cmOrderDirectories.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmOrderDirectories.h.body:
The header declares the `cmOrderDirectories` class that orchestrates the runtime ordering of library directories.  
It gathers directories from explicit, implicit, and language‑specific sources, resolves ordering constraints (including conflicts and implicit‑directory rules), and constructs a dependency graph to detect cycles.  
Finally it emits an ordered list of directories in `GetOrderedDirectories()`.

@l./Source/cmOutputConverter.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmOutputConverter.cxx.body: The file implements a helper that normalises paths relative to the top‑level source and binary directories, converts those paths into the correct format for the target shell (Unix or Windows) and for various build tools (make, MinGW, Ninja, VS IDE), and escapes special characters and variable references so that scripts generated by CMake render correctly in the target shell. It provides utility functions for quoting, quoting‑determiners, and handling of make‑variables and shell‑specific escape sequences.

@l./Source/cmOutputConverter.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmOutputConverter.h.body:
- Holds a snapshot of the build state to resolve relative paths.  
- Exposes `MaybeRelativeToTopBinDir` / `MaybeRelativeToCurBinDir` that return a forward‑slash path only when the source and target directories share a source‑ or binary‑tree prefix; otherwise they stay unchanged.  
- `MaybeRelativeToWorkDir` can be overridden to change the work‑dir target; by default it forwards to the current binary dir.  
- Supports three output formats (shell, Ninjamulti, response) via `ConvertToOutputFormat` and escapes them with `EscapeForShell`, `EscapeForCMake`, and `EscapeWindowsShellArgument`.  
- Provides a bitmask flag set (`Shell_Flag_*`) that controls quoting/escaping (e.g. whether the argument is in a Makefile, in a Windows shell, or contains `$`‑variables).  
- Determines whether a token needs quoting (`Shell_ArgumentNeedsQuotes`) by examining characters, `make‑var` syntax and special cases.  
- Computes a relative path relative to one of the known “top” directories (`ComputeRelativePathTop*`, `RelativePathTopRelation`).  
- Includes helper for C‑style Fortran line‑style detection (`GetFortranFormat`, `GetFortranPreprocess`).  
- Public interface ends with `SetRelativePathTop`, `GetRelativePathTopSource/Binary`, and `SetLinkScriptShell`.

@l./Source/cmOutputRequiredFilesCommand..author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmOutputRequiredFilesCommand..body:
The file implements a command that, given a source file and an output file name, writes the full list of header files that the source file depends on. It parses the source file for `#include` directives, follows each include recursively, and records each file that is required. The implementation is organized around two helper classes:  

* `cmDependInformation` – a small struct that keeps a file’s full path, its include name, and a `std::set` of other `cmDependInformation` objects that it depends on.  
* `cmLBDepend` – a helper that builds the dependency graph. It loads the include‑regular‑expression rules from the makefile, builds a list of include directories from targets, and then walks each file, recursing into each header it finds.

The top‑level function `cmOutputRequiredFilesCommand` creates a `cmLBDepend` instance, tells it the current makefile, runs `FindDependencies` for the requested file, and if any dependencies were found it opens the output file and serialises the dependency graph with the recursive helper `ListDependencies`.

@l./Source/cmParseArgumentsCommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmParseArgumentsCommand.cxx.body: The file implements the *Parse Arguments* command that processes a list of arguments and injects them into a makefile. It builds a `UserArgumentParser` that registers option names, single‐value and multi‐value arguments, and records any arguments that couldn’t be matched. The parsed arguments are then written into the makefile as definitions prefixed with the supplied prefix. The command also supports a “PARSE_ARGV” variant that reads arguments from the environment instead of a flat list.

@l./Source/cmParseArgumentsCommand.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmParseArgumentsCommand.h.body: cmParseArgumentsCommand parses a vector of command‑line strings into the internal representation of the execution environment, returning a boolean that indicates whether the parsing succeeded or failed. It records any parsing issues in a cmExecutionStatus object that callers inspect after the call. The header pulls in cmConfigure.h, which supplies the configuration context used for the parsing logic, and it relies on the standard string and vector utilities to iterate over the supplied arguments.

@l./Source/cmPathLabel.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmPathLabel.cxx.body:
The file defines a lightweight string‑wrapper class that stores a label string and a pre‑computed hash value.  
In the constructor the label string is hashed with a one‑at‑a‑time Jenkins‑style routine that repeatedly mixes the current hash with shifted copies of itself, mixing low‑ and high‑bit portions to keep the bits evenly distributed.  
The class overloads `operator<` to order objects by the numeric hash value and `operator==` to test equality solely by comparing the hash values. The header pulls in `utility` for standard utilities and pulls in the class’s own header `cmPathLabel.h`.

@l./Source/cmPathLabel.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmPathLabel.h.body:
The header file provides a lightweight helper class that stores a string label together with a pre‑computed 32‑bit Jenkins hash.  
Constructors take the label text; a single comparison operator (<) and an equality operator are provided to allow quick sorted lookups, but they do *not* impose any lexical ordering on the text itself.  
The class exposes getters for the label and hash, and is designed to be extended in other modules where a simple hash‑based key is needed for indexing or searching.

@l./Source/cmPlaceholderExpander.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmPlaceholderExpander.cxx.body: Expands tokens enclosed in angle brackets within a string by iterating from left to right, extracting the variable name, calling a lookup routine for its expanded value, and substituting the substring with that value while trimming any stray spaces that would otherwise leave consecutive blanks.

@l./Source/cmPlaceholderExpander.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmPlaceholderExpander.h.body:
The header declares an abstract interface for expanding template‑style placeholders inside a string.  
A concrete implementation must override the protected pure virtual **ExpandVariable** to resolve a single placeholder token. The public **ExpandVariables** method walks through the supplied string, replacing any placeholders it encounters by calling the derived implementation. The class is intended as a reusable component for any part of the project that needs to substitute runtime‑generated values into text fragments.

@l./Source/cmPlistParser.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmPlistParser.cxx.body: The file supplies a helper that runs the external plutil tool on a “.plist” file, reads the resulting JSON from the tool’s stdout through a pipe stream, parses it into a cm::json::Value, and returns that value wrapped in an optional object (returning nullopt when the conversion or parsing fails).

@l./Source/cmPlistParser.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmPlistParser.h.body:
`cmPlistParser.h` declares a single parsing routine.  
The header pulls in the standard `<string>` header and the project‑specific `cm/optional` helper, and forward‑declares the `Json::Value` type. The core function `cmParsePlist` accepts a file name and returns a `cm::optional<Json::Value>` – yielding a parsed value on success or an empty optional when the file can’t be parsed. The file’s intended use is in other parts of the project that call this routine to read a “plist‑style” JSON file into the `Json::Value` representation.

@l./Source/cmPolicies.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmPolicies.cxx.body: The file implements the policy‑handling logic used by CMake: it converts textual policy names (like “CMP0001”) into internal IDs, turns IDs back into human‑readable strings, and provides utility functions to decide whether a particular policy is “newer” than a requested policy version. It applies policy status changes (OLD, WARN, NEW) to the build system, emits diagnostic messages when an older policy is still requested, and keeps a PolicyMap that records which policies have been set to each of those states. The code also supplies helper strings and warning messages that describe how to switch a policy to NEW or OLD and the ramifications of deprecated behaviour.

@l./Source/cmPolicies.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmPolicies.h.body: The header implements the policy machinery used by CMake. It defines an enum of policy identifiers, a table that maps each ID to a string name, and a class that keeps track of policy states. The class offers methods for querying whether a policy is enabled, disabling a policy, and applying a policy to a generated makefile. It also contains helpers (macros) that iterate over all policies and emit compiler‑time warnings for unknown or unsupported policy values.

@l./Source/cmProcessOutput.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmProcessOutput.cxx.body: `cmProcessOutput.cxx` implements a helper that maps string identifiers ("UTF8", "ANSI", etc.) to internal encoding types, initializes the appropriate console codepage on Windows, and offers several overloads of `DecodeText` that convert raw byte sequences into Unicode `std::string` or `std::vector<char>`. The core conversion logic uses Windows‑specific APIs such as `MultiByteToWideChar` and `WideCharToMultiByte`, handling lead‑byte and multibyte sequences. The file contains conditional code that only compiles Windows‑specific code when `_WIN32` is defined, otherwise stubs are used.

@l./Source/cmProcessOutput.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmProcessOutput.h.body:
The header declares a small utility class whose job is to translate text coming from a child process into the encoding that the calling application internally uses.  
* Encoding support* – The enum lists the supported external encodings: `None`, `Auto`, `UTF8`, `ANSI`, and `OEM`. The `FindEncoding()` static function turns a string name into the enum value, defaulting to `Auto` when the name is unknown.  
* Configuration* – The constructor accepts an encoding choice and an optional `maxSize` (defaults to `1024`). When non‑zero, the decoder keeps any trailing incomplete character in a buffer that will be prefixed to the next chunk decoded, allowing multi‑buffer streams to be stitched correctly.  
* Decoding API* – Three overloads of `DecodeText()` accept: a `std::string`, a raw character buffer (`const char*` with length) or a `std::vector<char>`. All return a boolean success flag and write the decoded text into the supplied string. The private section keeps the codepage, buffer size, and a vector of string parts that accumulate incomplete fragments between calls.

@l./Source/cmProcessTools.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmProcessTools.cxx.body:
The file implements a small helper toolkit for launching a child process and piping its output through customizable parsers.  
The main routine `RunProcess` starts a process, reads its standard‑out and -error streams in a loop, decodes the data according to a supplied encoding via `cmProcessOutput`, and forwards complete line‑chunks to `OutputParser` objects.  
A lightweight `LineParser` base class offers a separator‑driven splitter that can ignore carriage‑returns and log each line via a user supplied `std::ostream`.

@l./Source/cmProcessTools.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmProcessTools.h.body: The header declares a small helper library for capturing and handling output produced by external tools. It defines an abstract `OutputParser` interface that accepts raw byte buffers and reports whether it wants more data. Two concrete parsers follow: `LineParser` splits data on a line separator and supports an optional CR‑ignore flag; `OutputLogger` simply logs each line with an optional prefix. Finally, `RunProcess` runs a process object, streams its stdout and stderr through supplied parsers, and returns control when both streams finish.

@l./Source/cmProjectCommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmProjectCommand.cxx.body: The file defines the implementation of CMake’s `PROJECT` command. It parses the command’s arguments, sets project‑level metadata (name, version, description, homepage, supported languages) in the makefile’s cache, and enforces policy checks (CMP0048, CMP0096). It also implements conditional inclusion logic via the `CMAKE_PROJECT_*_INCLUDE` variables and handles optional pre‑include files.

@l./Source/cmProjectCommand.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmProjectCommand.h.body: `cmProjectCommand.h` declares a single API function that accepts a vector of string arguments and a status reference, returning a Boolean flag to indicate success or failure. The implementation is expected to parse the provided arguments, perform necessary configuration logic, and populate the `cmExecutionStatus` object with diagnostic information. The header also pulls in the core `cmConfigure.h` header and pulls in the standard library headers for string and vector handling.

@l./Source/cmProperty.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmProperty.h.body: A single header file defines a `cmProperty` class that exposes a `ScopeType` enumeration listing identifiers such as `TARGET`, `SOURCE_FILE`, `DIRECTORY`, `GLOBAL`, `CACHE`, `TEST`, `VARIABLE`, `CACHED_VARIABLE`, and `INSTALL`. The file uses `#pragma once` and pulls in `cmConfigure.h` via an IWYU pragma. The enum is meant to be used as a tag for various scopes in the larger build system.

@l./Source/cmPropertyDefinition.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmPropertyDefinition.cxx.body:
The implementation provides a lightweight container for property metadata.  
The `cmPropertyDefinition` constructor stores the short and full descriptions, a flag for whether the property is chained, and an optional variable name to initialize from.  
The `cmPropertyDefinitionMap` holds a `std::unordered_map` keyed by a custom `KeyType` (combining name and scope). The `DefineProperty` routine inserts a new entry into that map with `std::piecewise_construct` and `std::forward_as_tuple` to construct the key/value pair in‑place; it skips the entry if it already exists. `GetPropertyDefinition` retrieves the stored definition or returns `nullptr` when no entry matches the requested name‑scope pair.

@l./Source/cmPropertyDefinition.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmPropertyDefinition.h.body:
cmPropertyDefinition.h defines two small helper classes used by the configuration system.  
*`cmPropertyDefinition`* stores the documentation strings for a property (short and full descriptions), whether the property is chained, and the name of the variable that supplies its initial value. It offers simple getter methods.  
*`cmPropertyDefinitionMap`* keeps a `std::map` keyed on a pair of property name and scope, mapping to a `cmPropertyDefinition`. It exposes methods to add a new property definition and to look up an existing definition, returning a pointer or `nullptr` when none is found.

@l./Source/cmPropertyMap.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmPropertyMap.cxx.body: The file implements a lightweight property map that stores key‑value pairs in an unordered map. It offers helpers to clear the map, set a name/value pair (removing the entry if the value evaluates to null), append a string value to an existing entry optionally as a string concatenation, remove an entry by key, and retrieve a value or the full list of keys. Two “Get” functions return the keys or key/value pairs sorted alphabetically for deterministic iteration.

@l./Source/cmPropertyMap.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmPropertyMap.h.body:
The header declares a small helper type that keeps a mapping of string keys to string values.  
It exposes methods to clear the map, set or append values, fetch a stored value, remove an entry, and retrieve the keys or key/value pairs in sorted order.  
Internally it simply wraps an `std::unordered_map<std::string,std::string>`; helper overloads convert raw strings to the `cmValue` type used elsewhere in the code.

@l./Source/cmQTWrapCPPCommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmQTWrapCPPCommand.cxx.body: cmQTWrapCPPCommand provides a helper that, when invoked from a CMake build script, runs the Qt moc tool on each .cpp file listed in a supplied source list. It produces a wrapped moc‑generated file for each eligible source, places that file in the binary directory, records it as a source for the build, and adds a custom command to generate it. The function validates that at least three arguments were passed, reports an error if not, and records the new list of generated files back into the makefile’s definitions.

@l./Source/cmQTWrapCPPCommand.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmQTWrapCPPCommand.h.body: The header declares a helper that runs a Qt‑style command line and reports its outcome via a `cmExecutionStatus` object. The function accepts a vector of strings (the command’s arguments) and returns `true` when the command runs successfully and `false` otherwise. The implementation pulls in `cmConfigure.h` and uses the standard `<vector>`/`<string>` facilities for argument handling.

@l./Source/cmQTWrapUICommand.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmQTWrapUICommand.cxx.body: The wrapper runs the UI compiler and moc tools on each source file listed after the first three arguments. It builds the corresponding header (.h), implementation (.cxx), and moc (.cxx) files, registers those outputs as dependencies in the makefile, and enqueues the custom commands that invoke the executables. The routine finally records the generated source lists back into the makefile definitions.

@l./Source/cmQTWrapUICommand.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmQTWrapUICommand.h.body: The file declares a single helper routine that receives a list of argument strings and a status object, runs a Qt‑based UI command, and returns a success flag. It ties together the configuration macros from `cmConfigure.h` with the Qt execution logic, exposing a unified interface for callers to trigger UI actions and report back their outcome.

@l./Source/cmQtAutoGen.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmQtAutoGen.cxx.body: The file implements helper routines for Qt‑tool code generation. It supplies utilities to merge command‑line options while handling value‑type options, escape text for shell usage, and create or merge option lists for moc, uic, and rcc. It also parses QRC files, runs rcc in a suitable directory, and normalises file paths for the generated output.

@l./Source/cmQtAutoGen.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmQtAutoGen.h.body: The header defines a helper class for Qt‑based code generators. It offers static utilities to fetch generator names, quote strings, parse file names and directories, merge option lists for UIC and RCC tools, and a small helper for listing QRC resource files. The `RccLister` class wraps the rcc executable path and options, exposing a `list` routine that gathers resource files from a `.qrc` file.

@l./Source/cmQtAutoGenGlobalInitializer..author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmQtAutoGenGlobalInitializer..body: The file implements a global initializer for Qt‐auto‑generation targets. It scans each local generator’s targets, identifies those that need Moc, Uic, or Rcc processing, caches the compiler features of the required tools, and creates or re‑uses global Autogen and Autorcc utility targets. The helper functions add utilities to those targets and manage the creation of per‑target custom targets.

@l./Source/cmQtAutoGenGlobalInitializer..author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmQtAutoGenGlobalInitializer..body: This header declares a helper that orchestrates the global Qt‐AutoGen setup. It wraps a nested **Keywords** type holding the string constants that drive the generator (e.g. “AUTOMOC”, “AUTOUIC”, “AUTORCC” and their executable/option forms). The main `cmQtAutoGenGlobalInitializer` constructor receives a list of local generator objects, populates maps that associate each generator with the target names to be added to either the global “AutoGen” or “AutoRcc” build groups, and exposes utility routines that create or fetch the appropriate CMake targets. Public APIs include `InitializeCustomTargets()` and `SetupCustomTargets()` which walk the stored generators to wire them into the CMake graph, plus helpers that locate compiler‑specific features via `GetCompilerFeatures`. Internally the class keeps a vector of per‑generator `cmQtAutoGenInitializer` instances and two maps that record the global targets for the two generator kinds.

@l./Source/cmQtAutoGenInitializer.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmQtAutoGenInitializer.cxx.body: This file implements the glue that ties CMake’s Qt‑specific generator tools to the build system. It orchestrates creation of Moc, Uic and Rcc files, registers the generated sources with the project, writes the metadata files that describe the generated artifacts, and sets up any custom targets required for the Qt toolchain.

@l./Source/cmQtAutoGenInitializer.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmQtAutoGenInitializer.h.body:
The header implements the helper that walks through the various auto‑generation steps that CMake performs for Qt projects.  The `cmQtAutoGenInitializer` class inherits the core generator (`cmQtAutoGen`) and owns the logic that

* queries the Qt version from the `moc` executable,
* builds the lists of sources that must be processed by moc, uic and rcc,
* registers those generated files as new targets, and
* writes the auxiliary “info” files that later stages use to decide which files have changed.

The helper keeps per‑configuration dictionaries (`ConfigString`, `ConfigStrings<T>`), and a small set of plain helper structs (`Qrc`, `MUFile`) to describe the various files that need to be produced.  It also contains the `GetQtVersion` routine that probes the compiler‑toolchain for the Qt release and the required minimum major version.  All of this wiring is encapsulated so that the rest of the build system can simply request “initialize the auto‑generation” and the initializer will create the required targets, emit info files, and expose the `Init*` and `Setup*` hooks for the subsequent phases.

@l./Source/cmQtAutoGenerator.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmQtAutoGenerator.cxx.body: This source implements a Qt‑based code‑generation tool. It parses a JSON‑style “info” file, extracts configuration values such as project directories and verbosity levels, and uses them to drive generation logic. The file supplies a simple logging facility that can be toggled on verbosity and color and writes messages to stdout or stderr. It includes helper routines for reading and writing files safely, comparing existing and new file contents, and creating missing parent directories. The main generator class orchestrates the setup, invokes virtual hooks for specific generators, and returns a success flag after processing.

@l./Source/cmQtAutoGenerator.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmQtAutoGenerator.h.body: The header defines a base class for QtAutoGen generators, providing logging facilities, file‑system helpers (read/write, compare files, create directories), and a helper class for parsing JSON info files. It declares abstract `InitFromInfo` and `Process` hooks that derived generators must implement, and exposes a `Run` entry point that uses those hooks to perform the generation work.

@l./Source/cmQtAutoMocUic.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmQtAutoMocUic.cxx.body: The source implements a job‑oriented system that parses Qt source files, resolves include dependencies, and generates the required .moc and .ui files. It defines a central class that orchestrates parsing, evaluation caching, and compilation jobs, while caching parsed results for fast reuse. It handles multithreaded worker pools, path resolution utilities, and error handling through its abort and logging facilities, ensuring robust dependency tracking and efficient rebuilds.

@l./Source/cmQtAutoMocUic.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmQtAutoMocUic.h.body: The header declares a helper that processes the AUTOMOC and AUTOUIC sections of a Qt build. It pulls in the standard `cm::string_view` type and pulls in a project‑specific configuration header. The core function `cmQtAutoMocUic` takes two string views (an info file and a config path), scans those entries, and returns `true` when the processing succeeds. This routine is invoked by other parts of the system to wire up the Qt moc and uic steps.

@l./Source/cmQtAutoRcc.cxx.author: AI Short Overview

@l./Source/cmQtAutoRcc.h.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmQtAutoRcc.h.body:
The header defines an interface for processing Qt-generated RCC files.  
The `cmQtAutoRcc` function takes the file path of a Qt UI `.ui` file (`infoFile`) and a destination path for the compiled resource file (`config`). It parses the `.ui` file, invokes the internal Qt RCC compiler (via the `cmRcc` helper), and writes the resulting binary resource header to the specified location. The function returns `true` on success and `false` if the compilation fails. It is used by build scripts to automatically generate the needed `.cpp`/`.h` pair for each UI file during the build process.

@l./Source/cmRST.cxx.author: AI Short Overview
@l./Source/cmRST.cxx.body: The code in **cmRST.cxx** implements a lightweight reST processor that reads document files, recognises a set of custom directives (e.g. parsed‑literal, code‑block, replace, toctree, etc.), and emits correctly‑formatted output to an output stream.
