@lcmFortranFile::~cmFortranFile@k_ZN13cm.body: The `~cmFortranFile` function parses a Fortran‑formatted file, builds an in‑memory representation of its records, and writes that representation out as an equivalent Fortran file. It uses the `asprintf` API to marshal data into Fortran record structures, handles comments and trailing spaces, and then emits the data in canonical Fortran format for downstream consumers.

@lcmFortranLexer_GetCurrentBuffer@k_Z31c.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranLexer_GetCurrentBuffer@k_Z31c.body: The function receives a scanner instance and, via an internal cast to the Flex‐generated `yyguts_t` structure, returns the `YY_CURRENT_BUFFER` macro representing the scanner’s current input buffer. It essentially forwards the scanner’s internal buffer pointer to callers that expect a `YY_BUFFER_STATE` value.

@lcmFortranModuleAppendUpperLower@k_ZL31.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranModuleAppendUpperLower@k_ZL31.body: The routine appends the module’s name in an upper‑case form together with its file‑type suffix to a string passed by reference, while also appending the original string unchanged to a second string. It first inspects the source string for one of three literal suffixes (.mod, .sub, .smod) to compute the extension length, then splits the input into name and extension parts, upper‑cases the name, and concatenates name+extension into mod_upper and the unmodified input into mod_lower.

@lcmFortranParser_Error@k_Z21cmFortranPa.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_Error@k_Z21cmFortranPa.body: Assigns the parser’s `Error` field the supplied message or a default string if the message is null.

@lcmFortranParser_FilePop@k_Z23cmFortran.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_FilePop@k_Z23cmFortran.body: The function removes the most recent file from the parser’s internal file stack, closes that file descriptor, and re‑initializes the lexical scanner to resume scanning from the next file in the stack. It first checks whether the stack is empty (returning `false` if so), then pops the top `cmFortranFile`, closes its underlying `FILE*`, deletes its associated lexer buffer, and finally switches the lexer to the buffer of the file that is now on top of the stack. This guarantees that after each pop, the lexer state correctly reflects the new current source file, preventing any cross‑file lexical contamination.

@lcmFortranParser_FilePush@k_Z24cmFortra.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_FilePush@k_Z24cmFortra.body: The routine opens a file for reading, initializes a new lexer buffer for that file, then pushes the resulting file‑context object onto the parser’s internal stack so subsequent parsing steps can consume the new input stream while preserving the previous buffer state.

@lcmFortranParser_GetInInterface@k_Z30cm.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_GetInInterface@k_Z30cm.body: Retrieves the value of the `InInterface` flag stored in the parser, indicating whether the parser is currently parsing an interface section.

@lcmFortranParser_GetInPPFalseBranch@k_Z.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_GetInPPFalseBranch@k_Z.body: The function returns true when the parser’s current position is inside a pre‑processor conditional branch that has already evaluated to false; it returns false otherwise.

@lcmFortranParser_GetOldStartcond@k_Z31c.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_GetOldStartcond@k_Z31c.body: The function simply returns the value stored in the parser’s `OldStartcond` field.

@lcmFortranParser_Input@k_Z21cmFortranPa.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_Input@k_Z21cmFortranPa.body: The routine pulls bytes from the file at the current top of the parser’s file stack, copies them into the supplied buffer, updates the flag that marks whether the last byte read was a line‑terminator, and injects a trailing newline if the file ends without one. It returns the count of bytes actually transferred (zero if the file is already exhausted).

@lcmFortranParser_RuleDefine@k_Z26cmFort.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_RuleDefine@k_Z26cmFort.body: The function adds the supplied macro string to the parser’s `PPDefinitions` set, but only when the parser’s `InPPFalseBranch` flag is false—i.e., it won’t be added while the parser is inside a false pre‑processor branch.

@lcmFortranParser_RuleElif@k_Z24cmFortra.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_RuleElif@k_Z24cmFortra.body: The routine sets the parser’s *InPPFalseBranch* flag whenever a pre‑processor `#elif` needs to be handled. It checks whether the current conditional stack (stored in `SkipToEnd`) still has a true branch, and if no other false branch has already been entered; if so, it marks the new branch as false so that subsequent parsing skips the corresponding code until the matching `#endif`.

@lcmFortranParser_RuleElse@k_Z24cmFortra.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_RuleElse@k_Z24cmFortra.body: When called, the routine first checks whether the parser is already inside a nested false pre‑processing branch (`InPPFalseBranch > 1`). If so, it simply returns. Otherwise, it inspects the `SkipToEnd` stack: if the stack is non‑empty and its top element is `true`, it marks the current context as false (`InPPFalseBranch = 1`); if not, it clears the flag (`InPPFalseBranch = 0`). This toggles the parser’s state between “skip this block” and “process normally” based on the current pre‑processor control flow.

@lcmFortranParser_RuleEndif@k_Z25cmFortr.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_RuleEndif@k_Z25cmFortr.body: The routine cleans up the parser’s state after an `#endif`. It first removes any pending “skip‑to‑end” marker that was queued, and then—if we’re in a false pre‑processor branch—decrements the counter that tracks nested `#else`/`#endif` pairs so that the parser knows the branch is closed.

@lcmFortranParser_RuleIf@k_Z22cmFortranP.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_RuleIf@k_Z22cmFortranP.body: The routine records that a new pre‑processor branch has opened—pushing a flag onto `parser‑>SkipToEnd` so that the parser knows the current branch is active and must not drop any of its guarded statements. This flag persists until an `#else`/`#elif`/`#endif` closes the branch, at which point the flag is popped. The routine therefore guarantees that when the parser later encounters the next closing token it will correctly resume parsing the appropriate branch.

@lcmFortranParser_RuleIfdef@k_Z25cmFortr.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_RuleIfdef@k_Z25cmFortr.body: When a `#ifdef` is encountered the parser records that a new pre‑processor branch has started by pushing a “false” flag onto its `SkipToEnd` stack. If the parser is already inside a false branch it simply increments the `InPPFalseBranch` counter; if the macro is unknown it marks the start of a false region by setting `InPPFalseBranch` to 1; otherwise it flags the current top of the stack as true, indicating that the forthcoming code should be skipped until the matching `#endif`.

@lcmFortranParser_RuleIfndef@k_Z26cmFort.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_RuleIfndef@k_Z26cmFort.body: When the parser hits an #if … #ifndef, it pushes a flag to mark that a new pre‑processor block is entered. It then checks if the current scope is already in a false branch; if so, it bumps a counter, otherwise it checks whether the macro is defined. If the macro is known, it marks the branch as false; otherwise it marks the block as to be skipped until the corresponding #endif.

@lcmFortranParser_RuleInclude@k_Z27cmFor.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_RuleInclude@k_Z27cmFor.body: The function processes an `#include` directive during Fortran parsing. It first guards against handling includes while inside a pre‑processor `false` branch, then verifies that the current source file is on the parsing stack. Using that file’s directory, it resolves the requested include name. If the file is located, the function records its path in the parser’s set of included files and immediately pushes that file onto the parsing stack so its contents are parsed inline.

@lcmFortranParser_RuleLineDirective@k_Z3.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_RuleLineDirective@k_Z3.body: The routine processes a preprocessor # line directive: it extracts the file name, skips non‑file markers (“\<built‑in>”, “\<command‑line>”), normalises Windows‑style backslashes to single backslashes, converts slashes to Unix format, and if the file exists it records the name in the parser’s include set for later use.

@lcmFortranParser_RuleModule@k_Z26cmFort.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_RuleModule@k_Z26cmFort.body: The routine guards against parsing in a pre‑processor false branch, then when not inside an interface it converts the supplied module name to lower‑case, creates a name token via `ModName`, and registers it in the parser’s `Provides` set so that the rest of the system knows that this module identifier is available.

@lcmFortranParser_RuleSubmodule@k_Z29cmF.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_RuleSubmodule@k_Z29cmF.body: The routine registers the fact that a Fortran rule’s submodule will provide a particular `.smod` file. It first guards against being inside an `#if 0`‑style false branch, then normalises the supplied module and submodule names to lower‑case, and inserts the corresponding module requirement and sub‑module provision entries into the parser’s `Info` data structures.

@lcmFortranParser_RuleSubmoduleNested@k_.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_RuleSubmoduleNested@k_.body: The function registers a dependency chain for a nested submodule within a Fortran parser: it normalises the supplied names to lower‑case, then inserts a requirement that the top‑level module’s submodule (identified by `module_name:submodule_name`) must be available, and records that the nested submodule will provide the same module identifier (`module_name@nested_submodule_name`). It performs this only when the parser is not in a false‑branch of a pre‑processor directive.

@lcmFortranParser_RuleUndef@k_Z25cmFortr.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_RuleUndef@k_Z25cmFortr.body: The routine checks whether the current parsing context is active (i.e., not inside an inactive pre‑processor branch). If so, it looks the given macro name up in the parser’s definition set and erases that entry when found.

@lcmFortranParser_RuleUse@k_Z23cmFortran.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_RuleUse@k_Z23cmFortran.body: The routine adds a module requirement to the current parser state. It first checks if the parser is in a pre‑processor false branch; if so, it exits immediately. Otherwise it normalises the supplied module name to lower‑case, resolves it to a fully‑qualified module identifier via `ModName`, and inserts that identifier into the `Requires` set of the current parsing context.

@lcmFortranParser_RuleUseIntrinsic@k_Z32.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_RuleUseIntrinsic@k_Z32.body: The function records an intrinsic module name in the parser’s internal registry. It first checks whether the current parsing context is a pre‑processor “false” branch—if so, it returns immediately. Otherwise it normalises the supplied name to lowercase and inserts it into the parser’s `Info.Intrinsics` set via the `ModName` helper, thereby tracking the intrinsic module that has been requested.

@lcmFortranParser_SetInInterface@k_Z30cm.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_SetInInterface@k_Z30cm.body: The routine updates the parser’s `InInterface` flag unless the parser is in a false PP‑branch, in which case it exits immediately.

@lcmFortranParser_SetInPPFalseBranch@k_Z.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_SetInPPFalseBranch@k_Z.body: The function assigns the supplied `is_in` value to the parser’s internal flag that tracks whether the parser is currently inside a pre‑processor false branch; it is invoked whenever the parser’s context switches into or out of such a branch.

@lcmFortranParser_SetOldStartcond@k_Z31c.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_SetOldStartcond@k_Z31c.body: Assigns the supplied integer to the `OldStartcond` member of the parser object, effectively recording the parser’s previous start‑condition state for later use.

@lcmFortranParser_StringAppend@k_Z28cmFo.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_StringAppend@k_Z28cmFo.body: Appends the supplied character to the parser’s current token string, extending the token being built.

@lcmFortranParser_StringEnd@k_Z25cmFortr.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_StringEnd@k_Z25cmFortr.body: The function simply returns a pointer to the parser’s current token string buffer. It exposes the internal `TokenString` as a C‑style string when the parser reaches the end of a string literal.

@lcmFortranParser_StringStart@k_Z27cmFor.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_StringStart@k_Z27cmFor.body: Clears the parser’s token string buffer so that no leftover characters from a previous string token contaminate the current token.

@lcmFortranParser_s::FindIncludeFile@k_Z.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_s::FindIncludeFile@k_Z.body: It checks whether an include name is an absolute path; if so, it returns that path. Otherwise it first looks in the directory of the file that contains the include directive, and finally scans each directory in the include‑path list until it finds the file, returning the full path when found.

@lcmFortranParser_s::ModName@k_ZNK17cmFo.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_s::ModName@k_ZNK17cmFo.body: The function takes a string reference and returns that string with the literal “.mod” appended, producing the name of a module file.

@lcmFortranParser_s::SModName@k_ZNK17cmF.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_s::SModName@k_ZNK17cmF.body: The function builds a module‑name string. It uses the compiler’s `SModExt` (defaulting to “.mod” if unset) and, if a separator is defined, prefixes the sub‑name with the separator after the base name; otherwise it simply concatenates the sub‑name and extension.

@lcmFortranParser_s::cmFortranParser_s@k.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_s::cmFortranParser_s@k.body: It stores the supplied compiler and tables in member fields, flags that the parser is not in an interface or false‑branch context, and then wires up the lexical scanner with the current scanner instance. Finally, it creates a short “dummy” buffer (size 4) that points at no data so that, when the input file stack is exhausted, the scanner can fall back on a harmless buffer.

@lcmFortranParser_s::~cmFortranParser_s@.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranParser_s::~cmFortranParser_s@.body: The destructor simply releases the scanner’s resources by invoking `cmFortran_yylex_destroy` on the stored scanner pointer. This cleans up the lexer instance that the parser had allocated.

@lcmFortranSourceInfo::cmFortranSourceIn.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranSourceInfo::cmFortranSourceIn.body: Retrieves Fortran source metadata—path, line numbers and related context—to aid downstream dependency analysis.

@lcmFortranSourceInfo::~cmFortranSourceI.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranSourceInfo::~cmFortranSourceI.body: Returns a struct that bundles the Fortran source file’s location, its origin (e.g., project or external library), and the compiler‑specific options used to build that file.

@lcmFortranSourceInfo@kc1cmFortranSource.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranSourceInfo@kc1cmFortranSource.body: cmFortranSourceInfo is a lightweight holder used during Fortran dependency resolution. It stores the file’s identity (path), its compile flags and a list of other source files it pulls in, and provides quick lookup helpers so that other components can ask for the file’s path or its direct dependencies without recomputing them.

@lcmFortranStreamContainsSequence@k_ZL31.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranStreamContainsSequence@k_ZL31.body: The function reads characters from the given `istream` one by one, comparing them against the supplied sequence. It returns `true` only when all `len` characters in that order have been matched; otherwise it returns `false`.

@lcmFortranStreamsDiffer@k_ZL22cmFortran.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortranStreamsDiffer@k_ZL22cmFortran.body: The function reads each stream byte‑by‑byte until a mismatch or the end of either stream is reached. If the two streams differ in length or content, the function returns `true`; otherwise it returns `false`.

@lcmFortran_yy_create_buffer@k_Z26cmFort.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortran_yy_create_buffer@k_Z26cmFort.body:
This function dynamically allocates memory to create a buffer state for the given file, with a specified size. Notably, it allocates an additional two characters for the buffer beyond the requested size, suggesting that the buffer is used to store characters in a format that requires extra space for end-of-buffer markers. 

The function uses two separate allocations for the buffer state and the character buffer, which could potentially increase memory usage. It also checks for memory allocation failures, which is a good practice for robustness.

@lcmFortran_yy_delete_buffer@k_Z26cmFort.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortran_yy_delete_buffer@k_Z26cmFort.body:
This function appears to be responsible for deleting a buffer in the context of a parser, specifically one generated by the GNU C++ lexer. It's worth noting that the function's logic seems to be focused on releasing memory associated with the buffer, particularly the `yy_ch_buf` array when the buffer is managed by the parser. 

The function's behavior when the current buffer is being deleted is unclear, as it's not entirely sure whether to pop the current buffer or not. This might be a design decision that depends on the specific requirements of the parser.

@lcmFortran_yy_flush_buffer@k_Z25cmFortr.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortran_yy_flush_buffer@k_Z25cmFortr.body: This function, cmFortran_yy_flush_buffer, appears to be designed for the scanner of a parser generator tool, likely a Fortran parser. Upon closer inspection, it's noticeable that the function does not simply reset the buffer, but also inserts specific characters at the beginning of the buffer to force a transition to the end-of-buffer state, indicating potential complexities in the parser's handling of buffer transitions. This suggests that the scanner's architecture is tightly integrated with the parser's state machine. The function also checks if the current buffer is the one being flushed, implying that there may be multiple buffers in use.

@lcmFortran_yy_init_buffer@k_ZL24cmFortr.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortran_yy_init_buffer@k_ZL24cmFortr.body: The function resets a `YY_BUFFER_STATE` structure to represent a fresh input source. It clears any existing buffer contents, stores the supplied `FILE*`, and, unless the buffer is already the current one, resets its line‑number and column counters. It also flags whether the input is an interactive terminal by testing the file descriptor with `isatty`. Finally, it preserves the original `errno` value across the call.

@lcmFortran_yy_load_buffer_state@k_ZL30c.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortran_yy_load_buffer_state@k_ZL30c.body: Copies the current input buffer snapshot into the scanner’s internal structure – it pulls the current character count, the buffer pointer, the file handle and the next byte to be consumed and stores them in the yyguts_t context.

@lcmFortran_yy_scan_buffer@k_Z24cmFortra.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortran_yy_scan_buffer@k_Z24cmFortra.body: This function appears to be a part of a lexical scanner (e.g., lexer or parser) and is responsible for initializing a buffer for parsing. It checks the provided buffer for a valid end of buffer (EOB) marker and allocates memory for the buffer state if sufficient. If the allocation fails, it issues a fatal error. Note that the allocated buffer state's position, size, and other attributes are set based on the provided buffer.

@lcmFortran_yy_scan_bytes@k_Z23cmFortran.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortran_yy_scan_bytes@k_Z23cmFortran.body:
This function appears to allocate and initialize a buffer for the input scanner based on a provided byte array. Notably, it preserves the original byte array's length and appends a trailing `YY_END_OF_BUFFER_CHAR` to indicate the buffer's end. The allocated buffer is then passed to `yy_scan_buffer` for further processing. 

It is worth noting that the function handles memory allocation failures robustly by checking for `NULL` and returning an error. However, it does not seem to handle the case where the input byte array's length is negative, which could potentially cause a buffer overflow if not handled explicitly. 

Additionally, the comment suggests that the buffer should be discarded after use, but this behavior is not enforced and may need to be implemented explicitly by the calling code.

@lcmFortran_yy_scan_string@k_Z24cmFortra.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortran_yy_scan_string@k_Z24cmFortra.body: This function, `cmFortran_yy_scan_string`, appears to be a thin wrapper around `yy_scan_bytes`. It leverages the `strlen` function to determine the length of the input string, `yystr`, which is then passed to `yy_scan_bytes` for parsing. This design suggests that the underlying parser is capable of handling dynamic string lengths. However, it's worth noting that the use of `strlen` may incur additional overhead due to the need for a second function call, potentially impacting performance in high-frequency or real-time systems.

@lcmFortran_yy_switch_to_buffer@k_Z29cmF.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortran_yy_switch_to_buffer@k_Z29cmF.body: This function appears to be handling a buffer switch for a parsing engine, but a subtle aspect is the handling of the `yy_did_buffer_switch_on_eof` flag, which is always set to 1 after the switch, regardless of whether it occurred during EOF processing. This may have implications for handling end-of-file scenarios.

@lcmFortran_yyalloc@k_Z17cmFortran_yyall.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortran_yyalloc@k_Z17cmFortran_yyall.body: This function, cmFortran_yyalloc, appears to be an implementation of a memory allocation function for the yyguts_t struct, but with a subtle twist. The function ignores the contents of the yyguts_t struct and only uses the yyscan_t pointer's value as a void pointer, which is then passed to malloc. This behavior suggests that the yyguts_t struct's memory is managed elsewhere, potentially by the scanner itself.

@lcmFortran_yyensure_buffer_stack@k_ZL31.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortran_yyensure_buffer_stack@k_ZL31.body: The routine lazily allocates a stack of `yy_buffer_state` pointers: if the stack is nil it allocates two slots, zeroes them, and sets the top and max counters. When the stack fills, it grows the array by eight slots, re‑allocates the buffer, zero‑fills the new region, and updates the capacity. If allocation fails it aborts with `YY_FATAL_ERROR`.

@lcmFortran_yyerror@k_ZL17cmFortran_yyer.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortran_yyerror@k_ZL17cmFortran_yyer.body: Retrieves the parser context from the scanner via `cmFortran_yyget_extra` and forwards the supplied message to the parser’s error‑handling routine (`cmFortranParser_Error`).

@lcmFortran_yyfree@k_Z16cmFortran_yyfree.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortran_yyfree@k_Z16cmFortran_yyfree.body:
This function appears to be a part of a larger scanner implementation, possibly related to lexical analysis or parsing. Upon closer inspection, it can be inferred that `yyfree` serves as a memory management function, specifically designed to deallocate memory blocks allocated by a `yyrealloc` function (not shown here). 

One subtle observation is that the function takes a `yyscan_t` type, which likely represents a scanner object. However, the actual `yyguts_t` object within this scanner is cast away using the `(void)yyg;` statement. @lcmFortran_yyget_column@k_Z22cmFortran_.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortran_yyget_column@k_Z22cmFortran_.body:
The function `cmFortran_yyget_column` appears to be a part of a parsing mechanism, likely from a C implementation of a lexer or parser generator. Notably, it directly accesses and returns the `yycolumn` value from the `yyguts_t` struct, which is tied to the current scanner `yyscanner`.

The implementation is straightforward, but it's worth noting that it doesn't modify the debugging state; it only observes it. The function's simplicity implies that the debugging state is likely managed elsewhere in the codebase.

@lcmFortran_yyget_extra@k_Z21cmFortran_y.body: This function appears to be a thin wrapper around the `yyextra` field within a `struct yyguts_t` object. @lcmFortran_yyget_in@k_Z18cmFortran_yyge.body: This function, "cmFortran_yyget_in", appears to be a thin wrapper around the underlying "yyin" file pointer. @lcmFortran_yyget_leng@k_Z20cmFortran_yy.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortran_yyget_leng@k_Z20cmFortran_yy.body:
This function, `cmFortran_yyget_leng`, provides a direct reference to the current input length, `yyleng`, through the scanner object `yyscanner`.

@lcmFortran_yyget_lineno@k_Z22cmFortran_.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmFortran_yyget_lineno@k_Z22cmFortran_.body:
This function, `cmFortran_yyget_lineno`, is used to retrieve the current line number from the scanner `yyscanner`. 

The critical observation is that it does not update the line number; it merely returns the existing value of `yylineno`. This implies that the line number is only updated when the lexer is in a valid state, and `YY_CURRENT_BUFFER` is set.

This function would fail to return the correct line number if `YY_CURRENT_BUFFER` is not set or is invalid, and returns 0 in such cases. 

A more robust implementation might explicitly update the line number if it's necessary to do so. 

This function's reliance on `YY_CURRENT_BUFFER` also implies that it's tightly coupled to the lexer's state management, which could make it harder to reason about and maintain.

@lcmFortran_yyget_out@k_Z19cmFortran_yyg.body:

@lcmFortran_yyget_text@k_Z20cmFortran_yy.body: This function, `cmFortran_yyget_text`, appears to be a thin wrapper around the `yytext` pointer. However, it's noteworthy that it doesn't perform any error checking on the `yyscanner` parameter. This raises a concern about potential crashes or undefined behavior if `yyscanner` is invalid or corrupted. Additionally, it's worth considering whether this function adds any value beyond simply returning the `yytext` pointer, as this is a common operation in parser implementations.

@lcmFortran_yylex@k_Z15cmFortran_yylexP1.author: AI Short Overview

* `Args` – the raw argument strings as they appeared in the file.  
* `Functions` – a list of `cmListFileFunction` objects that have been registered for this command.  
* `Policies` – a map of policy identifiers to policy objects that may influence parsing or execution.  
* `FilePath` and `Line` – the source file and line number for error reporting.  

When `operator()` is called, an implementation typically:
1. Validates each argument against the applicable policies in `Policies`.  
2. Matches the argument list against one of the stored `Functions` (often using a name‑to‑function mapping).  
3. Executes the matched function, passing the arguments and updating `inStatus` to reflect success or failure.  

This design keeps command parsing, policy handling, and function dispatch decoupled while providing clear diagnostic information.

The `cmGeneratedFileStream` class is a thin wrapper around `cmsys::ofstream` that writes to a temporary file and atomically swaps it into place of the real file.  
The public API is a small set of helpers:

* The two constructors – one default taking an optional encoding and another that accepts a target file name; the latter creates a temp file, opens it, and reports errors unless the `quiet` flag is set.  
* `Open` does the same but for an already‑created object; it only works when the stream is not already open.  
* `Close` flushes and, if the stream is still valid, performs the atomic rename of the temp file to the desired name.  
* `SetCopyIfDifferent`, `SetCompression`, and `SetCompressionExtraExtension` toggle internal flags controlling whether the temporary file is copied over only when it differs, whether the data is compressed, and whether an extra extension is appended to the temp name.  
* `SetName` and `SetTempExt` allow changing the target file name or temporary file extension after construction.  
* `WriteAltEncoding` lets you write a chunk of data using a different encoding and automatically restores the original encoding state.  

The destructor verifies that the temporary file was successfully written before allowing the original file to be replaced, and it deletes the temp file otherwise.

@lcmLinkedTree@kc1cmLinkedTree@f./Source.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmLinkedTree@kc1cmLinkedTree@f./Source.body: cmLinkedTree stores nodes in two parallel std::vector containers: the element vector `Data` holds values, and `UpPositions` stores the parent index of each node. A node’s “position” is the index in these vectors; the root has position 0, the first child has parent 0, and so on. The public `iterator` type represents a node. Dereferencing and member‑access operators (`operator*`, `operator->`) forward to the underlying data via `GetReference` or `GetPointer`. The iterator validates that its tree pointer is non‑null and that its position is within bounds before providing access. `operator++` moves an iterator to its child by following the stored parent pointer. `Push` adds a node as a child of the node referenced by a given iterator, appending both vectors. `Pop` removes a node, removing its data and parent link if it is not shared. `Truncate` discards all descendants of the root, restoring a single‑node tree. The API operates in constant amortised time thanks to the vector back‑push/pop operations. It is suitable for small‑to‑medium sized trees where random access and parent lookup are inexpensive.

The class also supports device‑specific libraries. It contains helper helpers such as `WriteDeviceLibraryRules()` and `WriteNvidiaDeviceLibraryRules()` that assemble the appropriate linker flags and command lines. The `FrameworkVersion` member is used for OS X framework support, which is handled by `WriteFrameworkRules()`.

At a high level the class simply emits the correctly‑structured make‑rules for the various flavors of libraries that CMake knows how to build, delegating the fine‑grained details to the helper functions listed above.

- **`RemoveUnCoveredFiles`** cleans up any entries that never reported coverage.  
- The private nested `XMLParser` encapsulates low‑level XML tokenisation.  

Overall, the class reads JaCoCo reports, normalises routine paths, and populates the coverage container while discarding entries that yielded no coverage.

The class implements the logic for mapping a target’s requested C/C++ standard to the actual standard value that will be passed to the compiler. It stores a pointer to the surrounding makefile and provides helpers that query that makefile for the target’s language, configuration and requested features. When a target is seen in a given configuration, the class examines the requested features string to determine whether the standard is explicitly set, or whether a feature implies a specific level. It then returns the appropriate standard string or reports that the standard is unknown. The main public operations are:

* `GetCompileOptionDef` – creates the compiler‑flag string for the requested standard.  
* `GetEffectiveStandard` – maps the request to the actual standard string that will be used.  
* `AddRequiredTargetFeature` – ensures a target has the feature that forces a particular standard.  
* `CompileFeatureKnown` – checks whether a compile‑feature is recognised.  
* `CompileFeatureStandardLevel` – determines the standard level implied by a feature.  
* `LanguageStandardLevel` – converts a standard string into a level value.  
* `CompileFeaturesAvailable` – asks the makefile whether requested features can be satisfied.  
* `GetNewRequiredStandard` – derives the standard that a new feature will enforce.  
* `HaveStandardAvailable` – verifies that a standard is available for the target.  
* `IsLaterStandard` – compares two standard strings to see if one is newer.  

The helper functions (`CheckCompileFeaturesAvailable`, etc.) are internal checks used by the public queries.

The `EnvDiff` class tracks changes to environment variables.  
- **AppendEnv**: Adds a batch of `KEY=VALUE` strings to the internal diff map.  
- **PutEnv**: Inserts or updates a single variable; if the string lacks ‘=’, the key is removed from the map.  
- **UnPutEnv**: Explicitly removes a named variable from the diff.  
- **ParseOperation**: Parses a modification command (e.g., “unset VAR” or “export VAR=…”) and updates the diff accordingly, returning success status.  
- **ApplyToCurrentEnv**: Applies the accumulated diff to the running process’s environment and optionally streams the changes to a supplied output stream.

- `cmsysProcess_Pipe_STDOUT` if a line was found in stdout
- `cmsysProcess_Pipe_STDERR` if a line was found in stderr
- `cmsysProcess_Pipe_Timeout` if the timeout was exceeded

The function also appears to handle edge cases, such as the process producing data that contains embedded newlines, and broken pipes. However, the specific behavior in these cases could benefit from further clarification or additional comments.

- It uses an internal Expat‑style parser and manages parsing state via Parse, ParseFile, and the three‑step chunk interface (InitializeParser, ParseChunk, CleanupParser).  
- Subclasses override virtual hooks: StartElement, EndElement, and CharacterDataHandler to process elements and text.  
- Error reporting is centralized through ReportXmlParseError/ReportError and a user‑supplied callback (SetErrorCallback).  
- Utility helpers such as IsSpace and FindAttribute aid attribute handling.

Key responsibilities:

* Escapes attribute and content values with `SafeAttribute`/`SafeContent`, which return a wrapper that performs the necessary escaping.  
* Handles line‑breaking and indentation via `ConditionalLineBreak` and `IndentationElement`.  
* Exposes convenience overloads: `Attribute`, `Element`, `Content`, `Comment`, `CData`, etc.  

The object never copies or assigns itself, and handles the opening‑closing of tags automatically in `StartElement/EndElement` and the helper helpers (`PreAttribute`, `PreContent`, `CloseStartElement`). It is a lightweight writer that writes correctly‑escaped XML to any `std::ostream` while keeping track of nesting depth for proper formatting.

The function frees any previously allocated buffer, allocates a new buffer sized to fit the incoming string (plus the terminating NUL), and copies the string’s raw bytes into that buffer. The key pitfalls to watch for are: 

* **Memory Safety** – `delete[] *variable;` assumes that `*variable` was allocated with `new[]`. If it was allocated with `new` or was never allocated, this triggers undefined behaviour.  
* **RAII Compliance** – If an exception is thrown while allocating or copying, the original pointer is lost, leaking memory.  
* **Null‑Check** – `variable` should never be `nullptr`; otherwise dereferencing it yields a crash.  
* **Copy Safety** – `strcpy` must be fed a destination large enough for the terminating `\0`.  
* **Future‑Proofing** – Prefer using a `std::string` member directly or a smart‑pointer to avoid manual new/delete.

@lcmsys::Directory::GetNumberOfFilesInDi.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmsys::Directory::GetNumberOfFilesInDi.body:
This function assumes that the directory is not very large, as it reads the entire directory into memory to count the files. It also assumes that the directory does not contain a large number of files with names that change during the execution of the readdir function, which could lead to unexpected behavior.

While it correctly handles errors that prevent the directory from being opened and errors that occur while reading the directory, it does not handle the case where the directory is very large and the readdir function is called with a large buffer size, causing a buffer overflow error. 

It also stores the error message in the `errorMessage` parameter if it is non-null, but the error message is always a duplicate of the error message that would be returned by `strerror(errno)`, which could potentially consume a large amount of memory if `errorMessage` is a large string.

@lcmsys::DynamicLoader::GetSymbolAddress.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmsys::DynamicLoader::GetSymbolAddress.body:
This function leverages the `dlsym` system call, which retrieves the address of a symbol from a shared library. However, the returned value is initially a `void*` pointer to data, requiring a union to reinterpret it as a `DynamicLoader::SymbolPointer` function pointer.

The function is `static`, so it cannot be invoked on an instance – it can be called directly as `LibPrefix()` from anywhere in the compilation unit, and since it returns a pointer rather than an owning string object it incurs no dynamic allocation. @lcmsys::DynamicLoader@kc1cmsys::Dynamic.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmsys::DynamicLoader@kc1cmsys::Dynamic.body:
DynamicLoader is a thin, platform‑agnostic wrapper around the OS’s native dynamic‑library APIs.  
It defines a `LibraryHandle` type that maps to the native handle (`HMODULE`, `shl_t`, `NSModule`, `image_id`, or raw pointer).  
Key operations:

* **OpenLibrary** – overloads take a filename and an optional flag mask.  
  * `SearchBesideLibrary` (0x0001) – on Windows, resolves dependencies in sibling directories.  
  * `RTLDGlobal` (0x0002) – on UNIX‑like systems, makes symbols visible to subsequently loaded modules.  

* **CloseLibrary** – detaches a library handle, returning success status.  

* **GetSymbolAddress** – looks up an exported symbol and returns a `SymbolPointer` (pointer to a function) or `nullptr`.  

* **LibPrefix / LibExtension** – expose the default “lib” prefix and “.so” suffix for that platform (used when building full paths).  

* **LastError** – exposes the last runtime error string.  

The class hides the underlying OS details, providing a single API for loading, unloading, and symbol resolution across Windows, macOS, HP‑UX, and POSIX environments.

@lcmsys::Encoding::CommandLineArguments:.author: AI Short Overview
@lcmsys::Encoding::CommandLineArguments:.body: This constructor performs a deep copy of the internal argument vector: it first resizes its own `argv_` to match the source’s size, then iterates over each element, calling `strdup` on the source string when present (or storing `nullptr` otherwise). It therefore creates a fresh copy of every C‑string, ensuring that subsequent modifications to either instance do not affect the other. The routine relies on `strdup` to allocate the memory and on the implicit assumption that it succeeds; it does not guard against allocation failure, and it does not free any pre‑existing data in the target vector. The implementation is straightforward but has a few edge‑case concerns: if `strdup` throws or returns `nullptr` due to allocation failure, the code will silently propagate that failure without signalling; in a standard C++ environment, however, this copy constructor preserves exception‑safety with respect to its own operations, as the only allocations are performed inside the `strdup` calls.

@lcmsys::Encoding::CommandLineArguments:.author: AI Short Overview

It uses `strdup` on each element and resizes the vector to `argc+1`. No other side‑effects or checks are performed.

@lcmsys::SystemTools::PathExists@k_ZN5cm.author: AI Short Overview

@lkill@kkill.author: AI Short Overview
@lkill@kkill.body: `kill(pid, sig)` sends the specified signal to the process whose process ID is `pid`; it returns 0 on success or –1 on failure, with `errno` set to indicate the error.

@lkwsysBase64DecodeChar@p@l./Source/kwsy.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysBase64DecodeChar@p@l./Source/kwsy.body: The function fetches the value stored at index c in the pre‑generated lookup table `kwsysBase64DecodeTable` and returns that value.

@lkwsysBase64DecodeTable@p@l./Source/kws.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysBase64DecodeTable@p@l./Source/kws.body: The `kwsysBase64DecodeTable` is a 256‑element lookup table that translates every possible byte value (0–255) back into the 6‑bit value that was encoded in a Base‑64 string. The table is declared `static const` so it lives in read‑only memory and can’t be altered at run‑time. In the decoding routine the table is accessed via an index into the current input byte (`return kwsysBase64DecodeTable[c];`), yielding the decoded value (or a sentinel such as 0xFF for an illegal byte). The table is used to make the Base‑64 decoder a single table‑lookup instead of a chain of conditional tests, which keeps the routine small, fast, and easy to audit.

@lkwsysBase64EncodeChar@p@l./Source/kwsy.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysBase64EncodeChar@p@l./Source/kwsy.body: The routine converts an integer value to an unsigned char, then retrieves the corresponding Base64 symbol from a pre‑populated lookup table by indexing that table with the cast value. The table must be large enough to cover all valid inputs; any out‑of‑range index will result in undefined memory reads.

@lkwsysBase64EncodeTable@p@l./Source/kws.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysBase64EncodeTable@p@l./Source/kws.body: The array holds the 64 printable characters plus a padding terminator used by the Base64 encoder to translate a byte value into its corresponding Base64 symbol; the lookup is performed by indexing with the byte value in the encoding routine.

@lkwsysProcessChildErrorExit@p@l./Source.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessChildErrorExit@p@l./Source.body: The function writes the current `errno` description into a dedicated error‑reporting pipe and then terminates the child process immediately. It copies the error string into a fixed‑size buffer, sends it through the write‑only file descriptor `errorPipe`, and calls `_exit(1)` to stop the process without invoking any C++ destructors or cleanup logic.

@lkwsysProcessCleanup@p@l./Source/kwsys/.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessCleanup@p@l./Source/kwsys/.body: When the function is invoked it first checks for an error state; if one exists it sets an error message (unless already set) and marks the process as in an error state. It then iterates over any child processes that have been spawned, terminating each and reaping them until the wait call succeeds. Afterward it restores the original working directory if it was changed, removes the process from the global notification list (unless it was detached), frees any allocated buffers, and finally closes all open pipe ends associated with the process.

@lkwsysProcessCleanupDescriptor@p@l./Sou.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessCleanupDescriptor@p@l./Sou.body: The function receives a pointer to an integer file descriptor. If the descriptor value is greater than 2, it keeps retrying `close()` until the call succeeds or fails for a reason other than `EINTR`. Once the descriptor is closed, it assigns –1 to the dereferenced pointer.

@lkwsysProcessClosePipes@p@l./Source/kws.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessClosePipes@p@l./Source/kws.body: The function iterates through the process’s pipe array, and for each file‑descriptor that is still opened it repeatedly reads from the pipe until no more data is available (handling EINTR interruptions). When a pipe is exhausted it removes the descriptor from the select‑set and performs cleanup, decrementing the count of open pipes.

@lkwsysProcessCreate@p@l./Source/kwsys/P.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessCreate@p@l./Source/kwsys/P.body: The routine creates two pipes—one for the parent to receive error reports from the child and one to signal when the child has entered its own process group. It blocks SIGINT/SIGTERM while forking, sets close‑on‑exec on the pipe ends, forks the child, duplicates the requested stdio handles, restores default signals, creates a new process group if requested, and finally executes the command. If any step fails it reports the error back to the parent via the error‑pipe. Once the child has successfully exec‑ed and signalled it is in the group, the parent resumes unmasking signals and records the new child.

@lkwsysProcessDestroy@p@l./Source/kwsys/.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessDestroy@p@l./Source/kwsys/.body: The routine iterates over every stored child PID. For each entry it calls waitpid in a loop that retries on EINTR, clears the PID slot when a child exits, and decrements the counter of remaining children. When the counter reaches zero, it closes the signal‑pipe end to stop further notifications. The routine also records the first error condition it encounters.

@lkwsysProcessExit@p@l./Source/kwsys/Pro.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessExit@p@l./Source/kwsys/Pro.body: Terminates the current process by calling `_exit(0)`—effectively aborting the program with an exit status of 0.

@lkwsysProcessFork@p@l./Source/kwsys/Pro.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessFork@p@l./Source/kwsys/Pro.body: The routine implements an optional detached‑fork sequence. If the caller requests detachment, it first forks into an intermediate process, which spawns the real child. The intermediate writes the new child’s PID back through a pipe and exits, after which the original process waits for the intermediate to finish and reports the PID. If detachment isn’t requested, it simply performs a standard `fork()`.

@lkwsysProcessGetTimeoutLeft@p@l./Source.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessGetTimeoutLeft@p@l./Source.body: The function computes the remaining time until a timeout expires. It obtains the current time, subtracts it from the supplied deadline, and stores the result in a `kwsysProcessTimeNative` structure. If the calculated time is negative or zero (and the `zeroIsExpired` flag is set) it signals that the timeout has already elapsed. If a user‑supplied zero timeout is requested, it forces the remaining time to zero. The return value indicates whether any time remains (0) or the timeout has expired (1).

@lkwsysProcessGetTimeoutTime@p@l./Source.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessGetTimeoutTime@p@l./Source.body: The routine updates a process’s absolute timeout if it hasn’t been set yet, then compares the process’s default timeout against an optional user‑supplied timeout. If the user timeout would expire earlier, it replaces the computed value and signals that a change occurred (return 1); otherwise it leaves the existing timeout intact and returns 0.

@lkwsysProcessInitialize@p@l./Source/kws.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessInitialize@p@l./Source/kws.body:
- Resets all pipe descriptors to -1 and clears select‑error and timeout counters.  
- Allocates memory for per‑command data structures (`ForkPIDs`, `CommandExitCodes`, `ProcessResults`), zeroing the memory and filling the `ProcessResults` entries with default state values.  
- Stores the current working directory in a newly allocated buffer (size taken from the compile‑time macro or a 4096‑byte fallback) and clears the error message field.  
- Sets the process state to *Starting* and marks it as not killed.

@lkwsysProcessKill@p@l./Source/kwsys/Pro.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessKill@p@l./Source/kwsys/Pro.body: The routine first stops the target PID with SIGSTOP, sleeping a bit on Cygwin if needed, then scans `/proc` (or falls back to a `ps` parse) to discover any child processes, recursively calling itself for each descendant, and finally sends SIGKILL to the original process—on some Apple kernels it even delivers a SIGCONT before the kill to avoid a rare race.

@lkwsysProcessRestoreDefaultSignalHandle.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessRestoreDefaultSignalHandle.body: Sets the handler for every signal that is defined on the build machine to the system default (`SIG_DFL`) by calling `sigaction()` for each one. This restores the process’s original signal dispositions after any custom handling has been installed.

@lkwsysProcessSetExitExceptionByIndex@p@.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessSetExitExceptionByIndex@p@.body: The routine examines a signal value and maps it to a predefined exit‑exception code and message stored in the process result array. It uses a `switch` over the signal, guarded by `#ifdef` blocks for each signal macro, and invokes the helper macro `KWSYSPE_CASE` to set the exception type and description. If the signal isn’t matched, it falls through to the default case, marking the exception as *Other* and storing the numeric signal value in the result string.

@lkwsysProcessSetNonBlocking@p@l./Source.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessSetNonBlocking@p@l./Source.body: Sets the O_NONBLOCK flag on the given descriptor via fcntl and returns a success indicator (non‑zero on success, zero on failure).

@lkwsysProcessSetupOutputPipeFile@p@l./S.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessSetupOutputPipeFile@p@l./S.body: The routine validates the file‑name, tears down any pre‑existing stream, opens the new file with read‑only‑write access (creating/truncating it), ensures the file descriptor is closed on exec via `fcntl(fd, F_SETFD, FD_CLOEXEC)`, and finally replaces the supplied descriptor pointer with the new one, returning success (`1`) or failure (`0`).

@lkwsysProcessSetupOutputPipeNative@p@l..author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessSetupOutputPipeNative@p@l..body: The routine first shuts the existing descriptor referenced by *p, then marks both ends of the supplied pipe with the close‑on‑exec flag via fcntl. If that succeeds it installs the pipe’s write end into *p and returns 1; otherwise it aborts and returns 0.

@lkwsysProcessTimeAdd@p@l./Source/kwsys/.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessTimeAdd@p@l./Source/kwsys/.body: Adds the two time structures: it sums the seconds and microseconds, and when the microseconds overflow past one million it rolls over into an extra second.

@lkwsysProcessTimeFromDouble@p@l./Source.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessTimeFromDouble@p@l./Source.body: The function takes a double value that represents a time duration in seconds, extracts the integral second part and the fractional part, and packs them into a `kwsysProcessTime` structure. It casts the integral portion to a 64‑bit integer for `tv_sec` and converts the fractional part to microseconds by multiplying by 1 000 000. The implementation relies on implicit truncation of the cast, so values that exceed the integer range or have insufficient fractional precision may lose accuracy.

@lkwsysProcessTimeGetCurrent@p@l./Source.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessTimeGetCurrent@p@l./Source.body: The `kwsysProcessTimeGetCurrent` function retrieves the current timestamp for the calling process. It first checks whether the compile target supports `clock_gettime` with a monotonic clock; if so, it reads the current time into a `struct timespec` and translates seconds and nanoseconds into a `kwsysProcessTimeNative` structure (converting nanoseconds to microseconds). If the monotonic path is unavailable, it falls back to `gettimeofday`. Finally it casts the native structure’s fields to `long` values, populates a `kwsysProcessTime` structure with the seconds and microseconds, and returns that struct.

@lkwsysProcessTimeLess@p@l./Source/kwsys.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessTimeLess@p@l./Source/kwsys.body: Returns 1 (true) when the first time value precedes the second: it first checks the seconds field and, if equal, falls back to the microsecond field.

@lkwsysProcessTimeSubtract@p@l./Source/k.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessTimeSubtract@p@l./Source/k.body: The routine computes the time difference between two `kwsysProcessTime` values. It subtracts the second timestamp from the first, adjusts for under‑flow in the usec field, and returns a new structure containing the resulting seconds and usec values.

@lkwsysProcessTimeToDouble@p@l./Source/k.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessTimeToDouble@p@l./Source/k.body: The routine simply turns a `kwsysProcessTime` value into a floating‑point seconds value: it adds the whole‑second field (`tv_sec`) to the fractional microsecond part (`tv_usec` × 1 µs). No validation or overflow handling is performed; if the fields contain out‑of‑range or negative values, the result will just be the arithmetic sum in a `double`.

@lkwsysProcessVolatileFree@p@l./Source/k.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessVolatileFree@p@l./Source/k.body: The function `kwsysProcessVolatileFree` safely frees memory that was allocated to a `volatile` pointer. It casts the pointer to a plain `void*` to silence the compiler’s `-Wcast-qual` warning and temporarily pushes a diagnostic suppression for Clang‑specific checks. The `free()` call then releases the memory. This pattern is used when the object cannot be marked as non‑volatile elsewhere in the code path.

@lkwsysProcessWaitForPipe@p@l./Source/kw.author: AI Short Overview
@lkwsysProcessWaitForPipe@p@l./Source/kw.body: The routine keeps an array of child‑process pipes open, repeatedly polling them (or using select when available). It pulls ready data, distinguishes normal output from a signal pipe that indicates child exit, clears finished descriptors, and reports the retrieved data or a timeout/abort via its return values.

@lkwsysProcesses@p@l./Source/kwsys/Proce.body:

The resulting value from `yy_nxt[yy_base[yy_current_state] + yy_c]` becomes the new current state of the lexer. This table essentially implements the transition logic of the underlying deterministic finite‑state machine that drives the command‑argument lexer.
